types.name: WebauthnAssertion
types.description:
WebauthnAssertion is one WebAuthn (passkey) assertion, exactly as the
 authenticator produced it — the four fields of an
 AuthenticatorAssertionResponse, unaltered.

 NOTHING HERE IS PARSED BY A BROKER AND BELIEVED. Kernel recomputes the signed
 bytes itself (authenticator_data || SHA-256(client_data_json)), reads the
 challenge out of client_data_json itself, and verifies signature against the
 credential's own public key itself. A broker that rewrote any of these four
 fields produces a proof that fails, which is what keeps "compromising the
 broker forges no identity" (personalauth.proto's header) true of this path
 too.

 NO ATTESTATION OBJECT, DELIBERATELY. This is the desktop-passkey arm of the
 identity decision doc's §3 — the one whose device proof is explicitly the
 weaker one, because Windows/Linux have no App Attest / Play Integrity. The
 public key therefore arrives as an ordinary jwk.Jwk (the platform's key type
 everywhere else, including CreatePersonalPrincipal) and is trusted only as
 far as the nonce binding makes it trustworthy: the IdP's id_token carries
 that key's RFC 7638 thumbprint as its `nonce`, so a substituted key has no
 matching login. App Attest and Play Integrity are named as follow-ons, not
 stubbed: both need live verification against Apple's and Google's own
 services, and a mocked verifier would be a device proof nobody could trust.

fields.name: credential_id
fields.description:
credential_id is the authenticator's credential id, base64url without
 padding. It becomes PersonalCredential.credential_id.

fields.name: authenticator_data
fields.description: authenticator_data is the raw authenticatorData the authenticator signed.

fields.name: client_data_json
fields.description:
client_data_json is the raw clientDataJSON the authenticator signed over
 the SHA-256 of. Kernel parses it for `type` and `challenge`; both are
 checked, and the challenge is what binds this assertion to one IdP login.

fields.name: signature
fields.description:
signature is the authenticator's signature over
 authenticator_data || SHA-256(client_data_json), in the encoding the key's
 algorithm defines (DER for ECDSA, raw for Ed25519, PKCS#1 v1.5 for RSA).

types.name: WorkloadLocality
types.description:
WorkloadLocality holds a parent's current locality token.
 Children present this token on refresh to prove they can still reach
 their parent. The parent rotates the token periodically and registers
 it here. The same token is shared by all of the parent's children —
 it proves reachability, not individual identity.

types.name: WorkloadRevocation
types.description:
WorkloadRevocation records a revoked workload identity.
 Kernel checks this on refresh — if the child's SPIFFE ID (or any
 ancestor) appears here, refresh is denied.

types.name: WorkloadRevokeRequest
types.description:
WorkloadRevokeRequest revokes a child workload's identity by SPIFFE ID.
 Only the parent (or an ancestor in the SPIFFE path) can revoke.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description: spiffe_id is the child workload's full SPIFFE ID to revoke.

types.name: WorkloadState
types.description:
WorkloadState tracks workload identity lifecycle — localities and revocations.
 Separate from ServiceHealth to keep health focused on operational status.
 All services have RW (for locality registration); kernel enforces that a
 service can only write its own locality entry (keyed by SPIFFE ID).

fields.name: localities
fields.description:
localities holds locality tokens for parent workloads.
 Parents update these periodically. Children present the token on
 refresh to prove they can still reach their parent.
 Keyed by the parent's SPIFFE ID.

message.name: WorkloadLocality
message.description:
WorkloadLocality holds a parent's current locality token.
 Children present this token on refresh to prove they can still reach
 their parent. The parent rotates the token periodically and registers
 it here. The same token is shared by all of the parent's children —
 it proves reachability, not individual identity.

fields.name: revocations
fields.description:
revocations holds revoked workload SPIFFE IDs.
 Kernel checks this on refresh — if the child's SPIFFE ID (or any
 ancestor) appears here, refresh is denied.
 Keyed by SPIFFE ID. TTL: 24h (longer than any token lifetime).

message.name: WorkloadRevocation
message.description:
WorkloadRevocation records a revoked workload identity.
 Kernel checks this on refresh — if the child's SPIFFE ID (or any
 ancestor) appears here, refresh is denied.

rpcs.description:
MintServiceToken — self-mint. An internal service exchanges its Kubernetes
 token / cloud proof (bootstrap) or a kernel-signed refresh/access token for a
 token bearing its OWN identity (sub = caller SPIFFE). Never calls OPA;
 S2S tokens are identity-only. Signs Ed25519.
 auth_disabled: the caller authenticates via credentials in the request body
 (kubernetes_token / cloud_proof / kernel-signed input_token), not a bearer header.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
MintUserToken — on-behalf-of (AZP). A broker presents the user's
 already-IDP-validated claims; kernel runs OPA EvalEntitlement on them, then
 signs a user token with sub = user and azp = the broker's identity (the
 broker attests the claims; kernel trusts azp). Signs Ed25519.
 auth_services: ["*"] because which delegates may attest a human login is
 per-delegate runtime config, not a compile-time literal here; the identity
 check that matters is Delegate.auth_broker_kinds containing the request's
 broker_kind, done inside the handler, exactly as doMintDelegatedToken
 checks grant.delegate_name. Empty auth_broker_kinds — the default — is
 refused, so this is a relocation of the former hardcoded broker allowlist,
 not a widening.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
MintDelegatedToken — standing delegation (Grant) mint. A delegate presents
 its OWN kernel-issued S2S bearer token (verified identity) plus a Grant id
 it holds. Kernel looks up the Grant, confirms the caller's verified identity
 equals grant.delegate_name, replays grant.claims into OPA fresh via the same
 EvalEntitlement path MintUserToken uses, intersects the result with
 grant.authorized_scope, and mints a short-lived access-only token: sub =
 grant.subject, act = grant.delegate_name, azp = kernel (AZP_KERNEL — kernel
 mints this directly, not on a broker's attestation). No refresh/offline
 token is issued; the delegate re-mints per use from the same Grant id.
 auth_services: ["*"] because any registered delegate may hold a grant (not
 just oauth); the identity check that matters is grant.delegate_name,
 done inside the handler, exactly as doMintUserToken checks the caller
 against a Delegate today.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
BrokerDelegateOfflineToken — runtime delegation, delegate half. The delegate
 presents its OWN kernel-issued S2S bearer token (verified identity) plus the
 code the user handed it. Kernel looks the code up, confirms the caller's
 verified identity equals the withheld token's act claim, burns the code
 single-use, and releases the Offline Token. The code alone is not
 sufficient — the redeeming identity is the security boundary.
 auth_services: ["*"] because any registered delegate may be handed a code
 (not just oauth); the identity check that matters is the withheld
 token's act claim, done inside the handler, exactly as doMintDelegatedToken
 checks grant.delegate_name today.
 Named Broker, not Redeem: "Redeem" is not in tacplus's closed verb registry
 and Broker is the registered canonical whose definition this matches —
 "coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties ... owns matching,
 relay, or completion semantics" — which is exactly the CliTokenBroker-shaped
 handoff the decision doc points at. The request/response message types keep
 their frozen Redeem* names.
rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

rpcs.description:
MintToken — exchange (RT→AT→ST). The caller presents a kernel-signed token;
 kernel VERIFIES it and mints the next tier per the 3-tier rules (a refresh
 can't directly mint a service token, etc.). service_auds mints AT + N ST in
 one call. azp is preserved from the presented token onto every issued
 token. Signs Ed25519. This IS the real exchange (replaces the former
 standalone TokenExchange service).
 auth_disabled: the token to exchange is carried in the request body.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
MintExternalToken — WIF. A proxy presents the user token plus opaque routing
 metadata; kernel runs OPA EvalProxyPolicy, then mints an external token
 (token_use = EXTERNAL, azp = proxy) carrying the policy's aud/extra_claims,
 and returns the resolved dst_url. The PROXY — not kernel — performs the
 off-cluster api.anthropic.com exchange. Signs ES256 (WIF rejects EdDSA).
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
MintClientToken — cred_pair bootstrap. A client (schematicctl, CI, admins)
 presents a JWT signed by its cred_pair private key; kernel verifies the
 signature against the cred_pair PUBLIC keys held in the per-namespace config
 (ConfigState below; the root namespace's config holds the root admin
 cred_pairs seeded from Config.root_cred_pairs), and mints a bearer token
 with the resolved SPIFFE subject. S2S here; the gateway fronts this as C2S so
 pre-tenant external clients (schematic CLI, CI pipelines) can reach it.
 auth_disabled: the request body carries its own proof (no bearer header).
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
CreatePersonalPrincipal — device-first registration (first launch). The
 device presents a JWT signed by the key it is registering; kernel verifies
 that signature against the public key carried in the SAME request, mints an
 opaque principal_id, and creates the PersonalPrincipal row holding that one
 credential. This is the bootstrap case MintClientToken does not have: there
 is no stored credential to look the key up by yet, so the key comes out of
 the request body and the only thing that proof establishes is possession of
 the private half — which is all the BODY needs to establish, because any
 person may create a personal principal (device-first, no signup). Who may
 carry that request to kernel is a separate question, answered below.

 Registration issues NO token. A registered device obtains one through
 MintUserToken with AUTH_BROKER_KIND_DEVICE, which is where the
 Delegate.auth_broker_kinds gate lives; minting here would route around it.

 NOT self-authenticating, and therefore NOT proxied to the outside. A device
 reaches this only through the personalauth broker, which calls it S2S:
 RPC_FLAG_SELF_AUTHENTICATES would make tacplus emit a NoAuth gateway proxy
 route, and an open route lets a client skip the broker entirely — which is
 where azp provenance, rate limiting and every future abuse control live.
 Dropping the flag deletes the route, so gateway's deny-by-default refuses
 the path; the generator enforces this, not a rule someone has to remember.

 auth_services: ["*"] rather than ["personalauth"] deliberately: who may
 broker a login is per-delegate config (Delegate.auth_broker_kinds), not a
 compile-time broker literal in kernel.proto. "*" says only "some
 authenticated S2S caller"; the handler requires that caller to be a
 delegate carrying AUTH_BROKER_KIND_DEVICE.

 The request body proof is unchanged and is a second, independent
 requirement: the caller must also hold the private half of the key it is
 registering, which is what makes the row worth writing.
rpcs.verb_definition: Bring a new resource into existence.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Mint; creates durable resource state.

rpcs.description:
CreateTenantUserLink records that two tenant-user identities are the same human.
 Both sides are proved in ONE request: the caller is an IdP broker that has
 just verified BOTH id_tokens, and both carry the same `nonce` — the value
 the client generated once and sent into both logins. The shared nonce is
 the whole proof: without it a stolen token for one side could be replayed
 on its own to fabricate a link to somebody else's account.

 Neither side's namespace is taken from the request. The people side is
 derived from the verified issuer/subject, exactly as MintUserToken's people
 arm derives it; any other side's namespace comes from OPA, the same
 authority that names it at mint. A broker therefore cannot name a tenant it
 did not just authenticate a login into.

 A DEVICE SIDE (identity decision doc §3) replaces one of the two logins
 with a WebAuthn assertion — see TenantUserLinkSide.device_assertion. The
 proof is the same shape and the same strength, with the shared nonce
 replaced by a pair of bindings in opposite directions: the id_token's
 `nonce` is the device key's RFC 7638 thumbprint, and the assertion's
 challenge names that exact login. Kernel verifies the assertion itself, so
 a device side rests on no broker's word at all.

 auth_services: ["*"] for the same reason MintUserToken carries it — which
 delegates may attest a human login is per-delegate runtime config
 (Delegate.auth_broker_kinds), checked in the handler.
rpcs.verb_definition: Bring a new resource into existence.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Mint; creates durable resource state.

rpcs.description:
BrokerPendingApproval is the DEVICE-ONLY APPROVAL check (identity decision
 doc §5). tacplus's generated (spec.rpc).requires_device check calls it; no
 product implements it, and nothing else in the platform verifies an
 approval.

 A pending approval is PROPOSED by the person through
 PersonalIdentity.CreatePendingApproval — a browser or an agent proposes —
 and is consumed here by the one thing that counts: a WebAuthn assertion
 from a device linked to that person. A browser IdP session, a delegated
 agent token and a tenant admin all fail this, however completely they are
 the user.

 Verb Broker, not Authorize. This is the shape BrokerDelegateOfflineToken
 already has on this service — look one single-use record up by its opaque
 id, verify the presenter cryptographically, burn it, release the result.
 Authorize is defined as an authorization decision with NO state change, and
 this one burns.

 On Mint rather than on a service of its own because every service in the
 fleet already holds a generated kernel Mint client (kernel is the
 token_minter), so the generated check needs no new client, no new route and
 no new deployment wiring in any service that declares a requires_device RPC.

 auth_services: ["*"] because ANY service may declare a requires_device RPC,
 so any service may reach this. Nothing rests on the caller's word about the
 approval: the record names its own person, its own method and its own
 request hash, and the assertion is verified against the credential kernel
 stores. What a caller IS trusted for is reporting which of its own users it
 is serving (caller_namespace/caller_subject) — a service serving that
 request is already trusted with it.
rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

rpcs.description:
MintX509Cert signs an X.509 certificate under a per-service intermediate CA.
 Authentication via bearer token in the Authorization header or input_token
 in the request body (for gateway-mediated calls). auth_disabled: handler
 validates authentication internally — accepts both bearer tokens and
 request body credentials.

 On each call, kernel:
   1. Extracts the service SPIFFE identity from the token's sub claim.
   2. Gets or creates an intermediate CA for that identity
      (signed by root CA, pathlen:0).
   3. Signs the caller-provided public key (cert_request.key) under the
      intermediate CA, with the SPIFFE URI as a URI SAN.
   4. Returns X509CertChain: leaf cert + intermediate CA cert in chain.

 The intermediate CA is unique per service, providing per-service trust
 isolation — only nodes of the same service verify each other.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
MintWorkload mints a child workload identity. Caller must be authenticated
 (bearer token). The child's SPIFFE ID is the caller's SPIFFE ID + "/" +
 workload_name. Kernel validates: caller is not terminal.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
RevokeWorkload revokes a child workload's identity. Only the parent (or an
 ancestor in the SPIFFE path) can revoke. The revocation is recorded in
 WorkloadState and checked on refresh.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Delete; invalidates credential/session/grant semantics without deleting a resource.

rpcs.description:
RevokeGrant revokes a standing delegation (Grant) at runtime. Only a party
 to the grant may revoke it: the user it acts for (caller sub ==
 grant.subject) or the delegate holding it (caller identity ==
 grant.delegate_name) — both are withdrawing authority they already hold,
 so neither needs a broader authorization model, exactly as RevokeWorkload
 restricts revocation to the identity's own ancestor. The grant record is
 marked (revoked_at_ms), not deleted, and the write is persisted to the
 kernel disk snapshot so it survives a restart. Every mint from the grant
 and every exchange of a token already minted from it is denied from that
 moment on.
 auth_services: ["*"] for the same reason MintDelegatedToken uses it — any
 registered delegate may hold a grant; the identity check that matters is
 done inside the handler against the grant record itself.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Delete; invalidates credential/session/grant semantics without deleting a resource.

rpcs.description:
MintDelegateOfflineToken — runtime delegation, user half. The USER calls
 this with their own bearer token to connect an agent (a Delegate) they own,
 replacing the redeploy that bootstrap-only Grant rows used to require.
 Kernel resolves the (delegate_name, delegate_namespace) pair, mints an
 Offline Token with sub = the calling user, act = delegate_name, and the
 user's fresh OPA entitlements intersected with the request's optional
 narrowing scope — and does NOT return it. The OT never transits the user's
 client: the response carries only a short-lived single-use code the user
 hands to the delegate, which redeems it S2S via
 Mint.BrokerDelegateOfflineToken.

 RPC_FLAG_AUTH_ANY_USER, not the service default of entitled users: any
 authenticated person may connect an agent of their own, and the authority
 that agent ends up with is not this call's to widen — the handler mints
 against the caller's OWN fresh OPA entitlements, narrowed further by the
 request's optional scope. A separate entitlement grant here would gate
 "may this person delegate at all", which is not a question the platform
 asks today; GetMyIdentity is annotated the same way for the same reason.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
Acquire attempts to take the lock named by key on behalf of holder_id.
 Non-blocking: a key already held by a DIFFERENT holder returns
 granted = false rather than parking the call. Re-acquiring a key the same
 holder_id already holds is idempotent and returns the token it already
 has, so a retried Acquire after a lost response does not deadlock the
 holder against itself.
 auth_services: ["*"] — any service identity may take a lock; the key
 namespace is the caller's to partition (callers key by their own identity
 plus a discriminator), exactly as any service may mint its own token.
rpcs.verb_definition: Take exclusive hold of a named lock, returning a fencing token.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; a hold is not durable resource state the caller owns, and it may legitimately not be granted — a refused Acquire returns granted=false, not an error. NOT Mint; the token is an index into server-held state, not a self-contained credential.

rpcs.description:
Release drops the lock named by key. The caller must present the
 fencing_token it was granted; a token that is not the current one releases
 nothing and returns ok = false. That is the stale-holder case — a holder
 that lost the lock (or never had it) must not be able to release the
 holder that has it now.
rpcs.verb_definition: Give up a lock held under a fencing token.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Delete; drops a hold without deleting the lock's key. NOT Revoke; the holder gives up its own hold rather than invalidating someone else's credential.

rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

rpcs.description:
GetMyIdentity returns the CALLER'S memberships. It takes no principal
 argument by construction: the principal is resolved from the token's sub,
 so there is no field an attacker can point at somebody else.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT List/Watch; returns one resource or not-found and must not mutate state.

rpcs.description:
RevokeTenantUserLink is UNLINK. It takes no owner argument, for the same
 reason GetMyIdentity takes none: the owning side of the edge is the
 CALLER'S OWN namespace and sub, out of the verified token, so there is no
 field pointing at somebody else's link. The request names only the peer to
 unlink from.

 Either side may unlink, which is what makes "the person may unlink a
 device, from any linked device or via the people tenant flow" (identity
 decision doc §3) true without a second surface: a /people/<pid> device
 token unlinks its own person edge, and a /tenants/people person token
 unlinks any of its device edges.

 NO RE-PROOF IS REQUIRED. Linking demands both credentials at once because
 it GRANTS reach into another namespace; unlinking only withdraws it, and a
 device is most often unlinked precisely when it can no longer be presented
 (lost, stolen, wiped). Demanding the link-time proof to undo a link would
 mean a lost device can never be removed. Recorded as a product default in
 the slice's decision doc, not a silent choice.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Delete; invalidates credential/session/grant semantics without deleting a resource.

rpcs.description:
CreatePendingApproval PROPOSES something that will need a device tap
 (identity decision doc §5). The caller is the person, or a tenant user
 linked to one, or an agent holding that person's delegated token — and
 proposing is ALL this does. The record it writes authorizes nothing until a
 device linked to that person signs it, which Mint.BrokerPendingApproval
 checks; that is why a proposer needs no privilege beyond being the user.

 It takes no principal argument, for the same reason GetMyIdentity takes
 none: the person is resolved from the caller's own verified claims, through
 the link registry, so there is no field pointing at somebody else's
 approval to create.

 What it pins is the EXACT request. rpc_method names one RPC and
 request_hash digests the exact request that will be made, so an approval
 for "transfer 5" cannot be spent on "transfer 5000": the generated check
 re-hashes the request it is about to serve, and a different hash is a
 different approval.

rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Mint; creates durable resource state.

BrokerPersonalIdentityMcpSession carries one Model Context Protocol session for PersonalIdentity over a
 single bidirectional stream: one complete JSON-RPC frame per stream message,
 request frames in and response frames out, for the life of the session.

 Generated, never declared: PersonalIdentity has at least one RPC_PRINCIPAL_MCP rpc, and this
 is the only channel those tools are reachable through. Bidirectional because an
 MCP session is stateful — it opens with an initialize handshake and holds the
 negotiated protocol version after it — so a unary call would repeat that
 handshake per tool call.

rpcs.description:
CreateTenant creates the tenant named by tenant_namespace (e.g. "/acme", or
 "/acme/sub" for a sub-tenant) with the given immutable constraints. The
 tenant must not already exist. Two-step: existence only — it returns the
 Tenant and nothing else (no config, no key material); bootstrap it via
 SetTenantConfig. Caller must be at-or-above tenant_namespace (ROOT "/" to
 create a top-level tenant).
rpcs.verb_definition: Bring a new resource into existence.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Mint; creates durable resource state.

rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Revoke; removes resource state rather than invalidating a credential or grant.

ListTenants returns the immediate child tenants of parent_namespace

rpcs.description:
GetTenantConfig returns the TenantConfig for tenant_namespace (its cred_pairs
 + oauth IDP + opa policy slices). Caller must be at-or-above the target.

UpdateTenantConfig atomically replaces the whole TenantConfig for

   - every cred_pair's entitlements ⊆ the tenant's ceiling (Constraints);
   - min-admin-credential invariant: the result must contain >=1 cred_pair
     entitled to administer the tenant (always on);

     still contain the authenticating cred_pair (two-step rotation).

 the enum — not config — is what fixes the IdP set.

services.name: Mint
services.description:
Mint is the platform's sole token authority and signing service, hosted by
 kernel — the cluster trust root. Kernel signs all tokens (S2S, U2S, refresh,
 external/WIF) and all X.509 certificates / workload identities. S2S-only
 (gateway fronts the client-reachable methods as C2S); kernel makes no
 off-cluster calls.

 This is the CLEAN consolidated surface (one service, was 4): the former
 kernel.Mint / kernel.MintClient / kernel.ExternalTokenMint / kernel.TokenExchange
 are unified here. azp is set ONCE at MintUserToken (azp = the broker's
 identity) and preserved unchanged through every derived token (AT from RT,
 ST from AT, and any re-mint/exchange via TokenMint).

 Tokens are signed Ed25519 (internal) except MintExternalToken, which signs
 ES256 for WIF assertion verification (Anthropic WIF rejects EdDSA).

rpcs.description:
MintServiceToken — self-mint. An internal service exchanges its Kubernetes
 token / cloud proof (bootstrap) or a kernel-signed refresh/access token for a
 token bearing its OWN identity (sub = caller SPIFFE). Never calls OPA;
 S2S tokens are identity-only. Signs Ed25519.
 auth_disabled: the caller authenticates via credentials in the request body
 (kubernetes_token / cloud_proof / kernel-signed input_token), not a bearer header.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
MintUserToken — on-behalf-of (AZP). A broker presents the user's
 already-IDP-validated claims; kernel runs OPA EvalEntitlement on them, then
 signs a user token with sub = user and azp = the broker's identity (the
 broker attests the claims; kernel trusts azp). Signs Ed25519.
 auth_services: ["*"] because which delegates may attest a human login is
 per-delegate runtime config, not a compile-time literal here; the identity
 check that matters is Delegate.auth_broker_kinds containing the request's
 broker_kind, done inside the handler, exactly as doMintDelegatedToken
 checks grant.delegate_name. Empty auth_broker_kinds — the default — is
 refused, so this is a relocation of the former hardcoded broker allowlist,
 not a widening.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
MintDelegatedToken — standing delegation (Grant) mint. A delegate presents
 its OWN kernel-issued S2S bearer token (verified identity) plus a Grant id
 it holds. Kernel looks up the Grant, confirms the caller's verified identity
 equals grant.delegate_name, replays grant.claims into OPA fresh via the same
 EvalEntitlement path MintUserToken uses, intersects the result with
 grant.authorized_scope, and mints a short-lived access-only token: sub =
 grant.subject, act = grant.delegate_name, azp = kernel (AZP_KERNEL — kernel
 mints this directly, not on a broker's attestation). No refresh/offline
 token is issued; the delegate re-mints per use from the same Grant id.
 auth_services: ["*"] because any registered delegate may hold a grant (not
 just oauth); the identity check that matters is grant.delegate_name,
 done inside the handler, exactly as doMintUserToken checks the caller
 against a Delegate today.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
BrokerDelegateOfflineToken — runtime delegation, delegate half. The delegate
 presents its OWN kernel-issued S2S bearer token (verified identity) plus the
 code the user handed it. Kernel looks the code up, confirms the caller's
 verified identity equals the withheld token's act claim, burns the code
 single-use, and releases the Offline Token. The code alone is not
 sufficient — the redeeming identity is the security boundary.
 auth_services: ["*"] because any registered delegate may be handed a code
 (not just oauth); the identity check that matters is the withheld
 token's act claim, done inside the handler, exactly as doMintDelegatedToken
 checks grant.delegate_name today.
 Named Broker, not Redeem: "Redeem" is not in tacplus's closed verb registry
 and Broker is the registered canonical whose definition this matches —
 "coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties ... owns matching,
 relay, or completion semantics" — which is exactly the CliTokenBroker-shaped
 handoff the decision doc points at. The request/response message types keep
 their frozen Redeem* names.
rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

rpcs.description:
MintToken — exchange (RT→AT→ST). The caller presents a kernel-signed token;
 kernel VERIFIES it and mints the next tier per the 3-tier rules (a refresh
 can't directly mint a service token, etc.). service_auds mints AT + N ST in
 one call. azp is preserved from the presented token onto every issued
 token. Signs Ed25519. This IS the real exchange (replaces the former
 standalone TokenExchange service).
 auth_disabled: the token to exchange is carried in the request body.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
MintExternalToken — WIF. A proxy presents the user token plus opaque routing
 metadata; kernel runs OPA EvalProxyPolicy, then mints an external token
 (token_use = EXTERNAL, azp = proxy) carrying the policy's aud/extra_claims,
 and returns the resolved dst_url. The PROXY — not kernel — performs the
 off-cluster api.anthropic.com exchange. Signs ES256 (WIF rejects EdDSA).
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
MintClientToken — cred_pair bootstrap. A client (schematicctl, CI, admins)
 presents a JWT signed by its cred_pair private key; kernel verifies the
 signature against the cred_pair PUBLIC keys held in the per-namespace config
 (ConfigState below; the root namespace's config holds the root admin
 cred_pairs seeded from Config.root_cred_pairs), and mints a bearer token
 with the resolved SPIFFE subject. S2S here; the gateway fronts this as C2S so
 pre-tenant external clients (schematic CLI, CI pipelines) can reach it.
 auth_disabled: the request body carries its own proof (no bearer header).
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
CreatePersonalPrincipal — device-first registration (first launch). The
 device presents a JWT signed by the key it is registering; kernel verifies
 that signature against the public key carried in the SAME request, mints an
 opaque principal_id, and creates the PersonalPrincipal row holding that one
 credential. This is the bootstrap case MintClientToken does not have: there
 is no stored credential to look the key up by yet, so the key comes out of
 the request body and the only thing that proof establishes is possession of
 the private half — which is all the BODY needs to establish, because any
 person may create a personal principal (device-first, no signup). Who may
 carry that request to kernel is a separate question, answered below.

 Registration issues NO token. A registered device obtains one through
 MintUserToken with AUTH_BROKER_KIND_DEVICE, which is where the
 Delegate.auth_broker_kinds gate lives; minting here would route around it.

 NOT self-authenticating, and therefore NOT proxied to the outside. A device
 reaches this only through the personalauth broker, which calls it S2S:
 RPC_FLAG_SELF_AUTHENTICATES would make tacplus emit a NoAuth gateway proxy
 route, and an open route lets a client skip the broker entirely — which is
 where azp provenance, rate limiting and every future abuse control live.
 Dropping the flag deletes the route, so gateway's deny-by-default refuses
 the path; the generator enforces this, not a rule someone has to remember.

 auth_services: ["*"] rather than ["personalauth"] deliberately: who may
 broker a login is per-delegate config (Delegate.auth_broker_kinds), not a
 compile-time broker literal in kernel.proto. "*" says only "some
 authenticated S2S caller"; the handler requires that caller to be a
 delegate carrying AUTH_BROKER_KIND_DEVICE.

 The request body proof is unchanged and is a second, independent
 requirement: the caller must also hold the private half of the key it is
 registering, which is what makes the row worth writing.
rpcs.verb_definition: Bring a new resource into existence.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Mint; creates durable resource state.

rpcs.description:
CreateTenantUserLink records that two tenant-user identities are the same human.
 Both sides are proved in ONE request: the caller is an IdP broker that has
 just verified BOTH id_tokens, and both carry the same `nonce` — the value
 the client generated once and sent into both logins. The shared nonce is
 the whole proof: without it a stolen token for one side could be replayed
 on its own to fabricate a link to somebody else's account.

 Neither side's namespace is taken from the request. The people side is
 derived from the verified issuer/subject, exactly as MintUserToken's people
 arm derives it; any other side's namespace comes from OPA, the same
 authority that names it at mint. A broker therefore cannot name a tenant it
 did not just authenticate a login into.

 A DEVICE SIDE (identity decision doc §3) replaces one of the two logins
 with a WebAuthn assertion — see TenantUserLinkSide.device_assertion. The
 proof is the same shape and the same strength, with the shared nonce
 replaced by a pair of bindings in opposite directions: the id_token's
 `nonce` is the device key's RFC 7638 thumbprint, and the assertion's
 challenge names that exact login. Kernel verifies the assertion itself, so
 a device side rests on no broker's word at all.

 auth_services: ["*"] for the same reason MintUserToken carries it — which
 delegates may attest a human login is per-delegate runtime config
 (Delegate.auth_broker_kinds), checked in the handler.
rpcs.verb_definition: Bring a new resource into existence.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Mint; creates durable resource state.

rpcs.description:
BrokerPendingApproval is the DEVICE-ONLY APPROVAL check (identity decision
 doc §5). tacplus's generated (spec.rpc).requires_device check calls it; no
 product implements it, and nothing else in the platform verifies an
 approval.

 A pending approval is PROPOSED by the person through
 PersonalIdentity.CreatePendingApproval — a browser or an agent proposes —
 and is consumed here by the one thing that counts: a WebAuthn assertion
 from a device linked to that person. A browser IdP session, a delegated
 agent token and a tenant admin all fail this, however completely they are
 the user.

 Verb Broker, not Authorize. This is the shape BrokerDelegateOfflineToken
 already has on this service — look one single-use record up by its opaque
 id, verify the presenter cryptographically, burn it, release the result.
 Authorize is defined as an authorization decision with NO state change, and
 this one burns.

 On Mint rather than on a service of its own because every service in the
 fleet already holds a generated kernel Mint client (kernel is the
 token_minter), so the generated check needs no new client, no new route and
 no new deployment wiring in any service that declares a requires_device RPC.

 auth_services: ["*"] because ANY service may declare a requires_device RPC,
 so any service may reach this. Nothing rests on the caller's word about the
 approval: the record names its own person, its own method and its own
 request hash, and the assertion is verified against the credential kernel
 stores. What a caller IS trusted for is reporting which of its own users it
 is serving (caller_namespace/caller_subject) — a service serving that
 request is already trusted with it.
rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

rpcs.description:
MintX509Cert signs an X.509 certificate under a per-service intermediate CA.
 Authentication via bearer token in the Authorization header or input_token
 in the request body (for gateway-mediated calls). auth_disabled: handler
 validates authentication internally — accepts both bearer tokens and
 request body credentials.

 On each call, kernel:
   1. Extracts the service SPIFFE identity from the token's sub claim.
   2. Gets or creates an intermediate CA for that identity
      (signed by root CA, pathlen:0).
   3. Signs the caller-provided public key (cert_request.key) under the
      intermediate CA, with the SPIFFE URI as a URI SAN.
   4. Returns X509CertChain: leaf cert + intermediate CA cert in chain.

 The intermediate CA is unique per service, providing per-service trust
 isolation — only nodes of the same service verify each other.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
MintWorkload mints a child workload identity. Caller must be authenticated
 (bearer token). The child's SPIFFE ID is the caller's SPIFFE ID + "/" +
 workload_name. Kernel validates: caller is not terminal.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

rpcs.description:
RevokeWorkload revokes a child workload's identity. Only the parent (or an
 ancestor in the SPIFFE path) can revoke. The revocation is recorded in
 WorkloadState and checked on refresh.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Delete; invalidates credential/session/grant semantics without deleting a resource.

rpcs.description:
RevokeGrant revokes a standing delegation (Grant) at runtime. Only a party
 to the grant may revoke it: the user it acts for (caller sub ==
 grant.subject) or the delegate holding it (caller identity ==
 grant.delegate_name) — both are withdrawing authority they already hold,
 so neither needs a broader authorization model, exactly as RevokeWorkload
 restricts revocation to the identity's own ancestor. The grant record is
 marked (revoked_at_ms), not deleted, and the write is persisted to the
 kernel disk snapshot so it survives a restart. Every mint from the grant
 and every exchange of a token already minted from it is denied from that
 moment on.
 auth_services: ["*"] for the same reason MintDelegatedToken uses it — any
 registered delegate may hold a grant; the identity check that matters is
 done inside the handler against the grant record itself.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Delete; invalidates credential/session/grant semantics without deleting a resource.

services.name: UserMint
services.description:
UserMint is the user-facing half of the mint surface (token-management
 decision item 7): a mint RPC whose caller is a PERSON holding their own
 bearer token, not a service. It is a second service rather than two more
 RPCs on Mint because a service declares exactly one caller surface —
 tacplus's ValidateServiceSurfaces refuses (spec.service_c2s) and
 (spec.service_s2s) on one service, and every downstream consumer (REST/proxy
 route emission, the registry's auth_model, collection.TrustOf) reads that
 single classification. Mint stays S2S and authoritative; this block carries
 only the RPCs a client calls, and the gateway reaches them through its
 ordinary generic C2S routing (package kernel, no hand-written front).

 Same physical service, same Java handler instance — only the declared
 surface differs, exactly as PersonalIdentity and TenantAdmin already sit
 alongside kernel's S2S services in this file.

rpcs.description:
MintDelegateOfflineToken — runtime delegation, user half. The USER calls
 this with their own bearer token to connect an agent (a Delegate) they own,
 replacing the redeploy that bootstrap-only Grant rows used to require.
 Kernel resolves the (delegate_name, delegate_namespace) pair, mints an
 Offline Token with sub = the calling user, act = delegate_name, and the
 user's fresh OPA entitlements intersected with the request's optional
 narrowing scope — and does NOT return it. The OT never transits the user's
 client: the response carries only a short-lived single-use code the user
 hands to the delegate, which redeems it S2S via
 Mint.BrokerDelegateOfflineToken.

 RPC_FLAG_AUTH_ANY_USER, not the service default of entitled users: any
 authenticated person may connect an agent of their own, and the authority
 that agent ends up with is not this call's to widen — the handler mints
 against the caller's OWN fresh OPA entitlements, narrowed further by the
 request's optional scope. A separate entitlement grant here would gate
 "may this person delegate at all", which is not a question the platform
 asks today; GetMyIdentity is annotated the same way for the same reason.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; credential/claim issuance, not durable resource creation.

services.name: FencedLock
services.description:
============================================================================
 FencedLock — the platform's only distributed mutual-exclusion primitive
 ============================================================================

 Kernel is the one service that embeds Apache Ratis; every other service that
 needs a lock calls this s2s surface rather than running its own Raft group
 (decisions/kernel-convergent-only-plus-fenced-lock-2026-08-31.md). This is
 deliberately NOT a state boundary: kernel state is CONVERGENT-only, and
 mutual exclusion is a different concern from how a map replicates — the
 conflation of the two is what produced the unreal CONSISTENCY_ATOMIC mode
 that was deleted before this was written.

 A fencing token is the Raft log index of the granting Acquire. It is
 therefore strictly monotonic across the whole lock service, never reused,
 and never decreases across leader changes. A resource owner stores the
 highest token it has seen and rejects any write carrying a lower one: that,
 not the lock itself, is what makes a paused/partitioned stale holder safe.
 A lock with no fencing token only narrows the race window; it does not close
 it.

rpcs.description:
Acquire attempts to take the lock named by key on behalf of holder_id.
 Non-blocking: a key already held by a DIFFERENT holder returns
 granted = false rather than parking the call. Re-acquiring a key the same
 holder_id already holds is idempotent and returns the token it already
 has, so a retried Acquire after a lost response does not deadlock the
 holder against itself.
 auth_services: ["*"] — any service identity may take a lock; the key
 namespace is the caller's to partition (callers key by their own identity
 plus a discriminator), exactly as any service may mint its own token.
rpcs.verb_definition: Take exclusive hold of a named lock, returning a fencing token.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Create; a hold is not durable resource state the caller owns, and it may legitimately not be granted — a refused Acquire returns granted=false, not an error. NOT Mint; the token is an index into server-held state, not a self-contained credential.

rpcs.description:
Release drops the lock named by key. The caller must present the
 fencing_token it was granted; a token that is not the current one releases
 nothing and returns ok = false. That is the stale-holder case — a holder
 that lost the lock (or never had it) must not be able to release the
 holder that has it now.
rpcs.verb_definition: Give up a lock held under a fencing token.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Delete; drops a hold without deleting the lock's key. NOT Revoke; the holder gives up its own hold rather than invalidating someone else's credential.

services.name: CliTokenBroker
services.description:
============================================================================
 CLI Token Broker — kernel-mediated nonce matching for CLI auth
 ============================================================================

 Each oauth instance opens a BrokerStream on startup. The protocol:
   1. OAuth sends Register (instance_id) — identifies this stream
   2. CLI auth starts: OAuth sends RegisterNonce (nonce)
   3. Browser completes auth: OAuth sends CompleteNonce (nonce, subject, claims)
   4. Kernel matches nonces, mints token, sends TokenDelivery back to the
      oauth instance that registered the nonce
   5. OAuth delivers the token to the CLI over the Session bidi stream

 Nonce registry is in-memory. Kernel restarts clear it (CLI retries).

rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

services.name: PersonalIdentity
services.description:
PersonalIdentity is the personal principal's own view of itself. It exists
 because kernel state RPCs are service-only (checkAccess denies user tokens on
 every policed graph), so a person cannot read their own registry row over the
 state plane.

rpcs.description:
GetMyIdentity returns the CALLER'S memberships. It takes no principal
 argument by construction: the principal is resolved from the token's sub,
 so there is no field an attacker can point at somebody else.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT List/Watch; returns one resource or not-found and must not mutate state.

rpcs.description:
RevokeTenantUserLink is UNLINK. It takes no owner argument, for the same
 reason GetMyIdentity takes none: the owning side of the edge is the
 CALLER'S OWN namespace and sub, out of the verified token, so there is no
 field pointing at somebody else's link. The request names only the peer to
 unlink from.

 Either side may unlink, which is what makes "the person may unlink a
 device, from any linked device or via the people tenant flow" (identity
 decision doc §3) true without a second surface: a /people/<pid> device
 token unlinks its own person edge, and a /tenants/people person token
 unlinks any of its device edges.

 NO RE-PROOF IS REQUIRED. Linking demands both credentials at once because
 it GRANTS reach into another namespace; unlinking only withdraws it, and a
 device is most often unlinked precisely when it can no longer be presented
 (lost, stolen, wiped). Demanding the link-time proof to undo a link would
 mean a lost device can never be removed. Recorded as a product default in
 the slice's decision doc, not a silent choice.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Delete; invalidates credential/session/grant semantics without deleting a resource.

rpcs.description:
CreatePendingApproval PROPOSES something that will need a device tap
 (identity decision doc §5). The caller is the person, or a tenant user
 linked to one, or an agent holding that person's delegated token — and
 proposing is ALL this does. The record it writes authorizes nothing until a
 device linked to that person signs it, which Mint.BrokerPendingApproval
 checks; that is why a proposer needs no privilege beyond being the user.

 It takes no principal argument, for the same reason GetMyIdentity takes
 none: the person is resolved from the caller's own verified claims, through
 the link registry, so there is no field pointing at somebody else's
 approval to create.

 What it pins is the EXACT request. rpc_method names one RPC and
 request_hash digests the exact request that will be made, so an approval
 for "transfer 5" cannot be spent on "transfer 5000": the generated check
 re-hashes the request it is about to serve, and a different hash is a
 different approval.
rpcs.verb_definition: Bring a new resource into existence.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Mint; creates durable resource state.

rpcs.description:
BrokerPersonalIdentityMcpSession carries one Model Context Protocol session for PersonalIdentity over a
 single bidirectional stream: one complete JSON-RPC frame per stream message,
 request frames in and response frames out, for the life of the session.

 Generated, never declared: PersonalIdentity has at least one RPC_PRINCIPAL_MCP rpc, and this
 is the only channel those tools are reachable through. Bidirectional because an
 MCP session is stateful — it opens with an initialize handshake and holds the
 negotiated protocol version after it — so a unary call would repeat that
 handshake per tool call.
rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

services.name: TenantAdmin
services.description:
TenantAdmin is kernel's tenant/project control plane. There is no separate
 cluster-admin service: the namespace tree is uniform (ROOT "/" + tenants +
 projects) and every RPC is ordinary C2S, gated by the single generated
 entitlement authorizer, which enforces the level-or-below rule (caller must be
 at-or-above the target namespace) declaratively via each method's
 target_namespace_field. A caller entitled at ROOT manages top-level tenants; a
 tenant admin manages its own subtree. Handlers trust the inbound namespace
 strings (authorization already happened in the interceptor).

rpcs.description:
CreateTenant creates the tenant named by tenant_namespace (e.g. "/acme", or
 "/acme/sub" for a sub-tenant) with the given immutable constraints. The
 tenant must not already exist. Two-step: existence only — it returns the
 Tenant and nothing else (no config, no key material); bootstrap it via
 SetTenantConfig. Caller must be at-or-above tenant_namespace (ROOT "/" to
 create a top-level tenant).
rpcs.verb_definition: Bring a new resource into existence.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Mint; creates durable resource state.

rpcs.description: DeleteTenant removes the tenant named by tenant_namespace and all its state.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Revoke; removes resource state rather than invalidating a credential or grant.

rpcs.description:
ListTenants returns the immediate child tenants of parent_namespace
 (ROOT "/" lists top-level tenants), one bounded page at a time.
rpcs.verb_definition: Finite/paginated set, ordered by order_by; filters are fields.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Get-plural/Search/Query; collection reads must declare method_collection.

rpcs.description:
GetTenantConfig returns the TenantConfig for tenant_namespace (its cred_pairs
 + oauth IDP + opa policy slices). Caller must be at-or-above the target.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT List/Watch; returns one resource or not-found and must not mutate state.

rpcs.description:
UpdateTenantConfig atomically replaces the whole TenantConfig for
 tenant_namespace. Caller must be at-or-above the target. cred_pair
 management happens here (add = include the public key; remove = omit it) —
 this single atomic write path is where constraints are validated:
   - every cred_pair's entitlements ⊆ the tenant's ceiling (Constraints);
   - min-admin-credential invariant: the result must contain >=1 cred_pair
     entitled to administer the tenant (always on);
   - self-lockout guard: when acting on its own tenant, the result must
     still contain the authenticating cred_pair (two-step rotation).
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Merge; changes one existing resource rather than combining resources.

rpcs.description:
GetProjectConfig returns the (currently empty) ProjectConfig for
 project_namespace ("/tenant/project") — its presence records existence.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT List/Watch; returns one resource or not-found and must not mutate state.

rpcs.description:
UpdateProjectConfig atomically replaces the ProjectConfig for project_namespace
 (currently empty — used to create a project by establishing its existence).
 "/tenant/default" is auto-created empty at tenant creation.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Merge; changes one existing resource rather than combining resources.

rpcs.description:

rpcs.description: DeleteProject removes the project named by project_namespace and its state.

rpcs.description:
BrokerTenantAdminMcpSession carries one Model Context Protocol session for TenantAdmin over a
 single bidirectional stream: one complete JSON-RPC frame per stream message,
 request frames in and response frames out, for the life of the session.

 Generated, never declared: TenantAdmin has at least one RPC_PRINCIPAL_MCP rpc, and this
 is the only channel those tools are reachable through. Bidirectional because an
 MCP session is stateful — it opens with an initialize handshake and holds the
 negotiated protocol version after it — so a unary call would repeat that
 handshake per tool call.
rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

types.name: Config
types.description: Config is rendered by operator and mounted into kmaker at startup.

fields.name: cluster_name
fields.description: cluster_name is the logical Schematic cluster this kmaker signs for.

fields.name: listener
fields.description: listener is the gRPC bind address for kmaker.

message.name: Host
message.description:
Host identifies a network endpoint by hostname/IP and port.
 The host field accepts either an FQDN or an IP address (v4/v6).

fields.name: host
fields.description: Hostname or IP address (e.g. "api.example.com" or "10.0.0.1").
constraints: must be a valid hostname or IP address

fields.name: port
fields.description: Port number (1-65535).
constraints: must be a valid network port (1-65535)

fields.name: protocol
fields.description: Transport protocol. Default TCP (zero value).

fields.name: logger
fields.description: logger configures kmaker process logging.

message.name: LoggerConfig
message.description:
LoggerConfig represents the configuration for a logger instance.
 It controls the output format, verbosity level, and formatting options.

 Example usage:
   - Development mode with console output and pretty printing for local debugging
   - Production mode with JSON output and no pretty printing for log aggregation

fields.name: name
fields.description: Name is the logger name/component identifier

fields.name: format
fields.description:
Format determines the output format for log messages (JSON or console)
 Default: FORMAT_JSON in production, FORMAT_CONSOLE in development

enum_values.name: FORMAT_JSON
enum_values.description: FORMAT_JSON outputs logs as JSON objects, ideal for structured logging and log aggregation systems

enum_values.name: FORMAT_CONSOLE
enum_values.description: FORMAT_CONSOLE outputs logs in a human-readable console format, ideal for development and debugging

fields.name: level
fields.description:
Level sets the minimum severity level for log messages to be output
 Messages below this level will be filtered out
 Default: LEVEL_INFO in production, LEVEL_DEBUG in development

enum_values.name: LEVEL_TRACE
enum_values.description: LEVEL_TRACE is the most verbose log level, used for detailed debugging information

enum_values.name: LEVEL_DEBUG
enum_values.description: LEVEL_DEBUG is used for debugging information, less verbose than trace

enum_values.name: LEVEL_INFO
enum_values.description: LEVEL_INFO is used for informational messages about normal operations

enum_values.name: LEVEL_WARN
enum_values.description: LEVEL_WARN is used for warning messages about potentially problematic situations

enum_values.name: LEVEL_ERROR
enum_values.description: LEVEL_ERROR is used for error messages about failures and problems

fields.name: development
fields.description:
Development enables development mode which:
   - Uses console format by default
   - Enables stack traces for warnings and errors
   - Uses more human-readable timestamps
 Default: false (production mode)

fields.name: pretty_print
fields.description:
PrettyPrint enables pretty-printed output for JSON format
 This makes JSON logs more readable but increases output size
 Should be disabled in production for performance
 Default: false

fields.name: output_paths
fields.description:
OutputPaths is a list of file paths or URLs to write logs to
 Use "stdout" or "stderr" for console output
 Example: ["stdout", "/var/log/app.log"]
constraints: must be a valid file path (type: PATH_ANY)

fields.name: error_output_paths
fields.description:
ErrorOutputPaths is a list of file paths or URLs to write error logs to
 Use "stderr" for console error output
 Example: ["stderr", "/var/log/app-errors.log"]
constraints: must be a valid file path (type: PATH_ANY)

fields.name: disable_caller
fields.description:
DisableCaller disables automatic inclusion of caller information (file:line) in log entries
 Default: false (caller information is included)

fields.name: disable_stacktrace
fields.description:
DisableStacktrace disables automatic stacktraces for error-level and above log entries
 Default: false (stacktraces are included for errors)

fields.name: initial_fields
cluster_ca
fields.description: cluster_ca holds trust anchors that kernel nodes should trust.

message.name: X509Cert
message.description:
ProtoCert represents an X.509 certificate.
 The certificate is stored as a base64-encoded PEM block.
 Use NewProtoCert() in Go with DER-encoded certificate bytes to create.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is a unique identifier for the certificate

fields.name: base64
fields.description: Base64 contains the base64url-encoded PEM certificate block

fields.name: signing_ca
fields.description:
signing_ca is the cluster signing CA used to issue kernel certificates.
 The private key is present in the mounted kmaker config and must be backed
 by a Kubernetes Secret owned by operator.

message.name: X509CertChain
message.description:
X509CertChain contains a certificate chain and optional private key.
 chain[0] is the leaf (end-entity) cert, followed by intermediates, ordered toward root.
 When key is present, the chain is a full credential suitable for TLS.

fields.name: chain
fields.description: chain[0] is the leaf (end-entity) cert, followed by intermediates, ordered toward root.

fields.name: key
fields.description: optional private key for the leaf cert; present when chain is a full credential.

message.name: Key
message.description: Key represents a private cryptographic key (alias for ProtoKey).

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is a unique identifier for the key (corresponds to kid in JWK)

fields.name: base64
fields.description: Base64 contains the base64url-encoded PEM private key block

fields.name: created
fields.description:
Created is the Unix epoch timestamp (seconds) when the key was created
 Valid range: 1735689600 (2025-01-01) to 8045740800 (2225-01-01)

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is an optional stable key for chain collections.

fields.name: spiffe_prefix
fields.description:
spiffe_prefix is the SPIFFE trust domain for kernel SPIFFE URI SANs: the
 URI authority, so it must not contain '/'. Certificates minted here
 receive spiffe://<spiffe_prefix>/kernel. Operator supplies this from
 operator.Config.spiffe_prefix.

fields.name: token_audience
fields.description: token_audience is the required Kubernetes TokenReview audience.

fields.name: kernel_service_accounts
fields.description:
kernel_service_accounts are Kubernetes service accounts allowed to request
 kernel certificates. Empty means namespace=schematic, name=kernel.

fields.name: kernel_cert_lifetime_seconds
fields.description: kernel_cert_lifetime_seconds caps issued kernel certificate lifetimes.

fields.name: tls
fields.description:
tls is the optional serving certificate for kmaker's own gRPC listener.
 When unset, kmaker starts without transport TLS for local/dev only.

fields.name: health_probe_port
fields.description:
health_probe_port is the plaintext gRPC port for k8s health probes.
 Kmaker's hand-written bootstrap bypasses the generated ServiceManager,
 so this field must be on Kmaker.Config (not only on Grpcconfig.Config).
 Default matches the platform-wide health probe port.

types.name: EventBusRecordMeta
LetsEncryptCert
types.description:
LetsEncryptCert is the cluster's Let's Encrypt certificate set, held durably
 by stratum. It is the ONLY durable copy: LetsEncryptState above is a live
 in-memory mirror of it, kept for the gateway's benefit, and kernel is not a
 durability layer (decisions/
 kernel-no-durability-user-data-to-stratum-2026-09-25.md item 4).

 The write order is the whole design: obtain or renew -> write THIS record ->
 write LetsEncryptState.cert_data. A crash between the two costs nothing but a
 stale mirror, which the next start rebuilds from here. The reverse order would
 make a mirror that outlives its own durable copy, which is the shape the
 kernel-persistence experiment had.

 ONE ROW PER HOSTNAME SET, not one row per issuance: certmagic manages a single
 multi-SAN certificate for Config.hostnames, so a renewal REPLACES this row
 rather than appending beside it (hence MUTABILITY_CRUD, the default). The
 record is not an issuance log and must not become one — the previous
 certificate is of no use to anyone once the new one is live.

 THE ACME ACCOUNT TRAVELS WITH IT. certmagic_state below is the whole storage
 tree, account registration and account key included, so the account is durable
 for exactly as long as the certificate it issued is. Splitting the account into
 a record of its own would let the two get out of step, and an account that
 outlives nothing is one more ACME registration against Let's Encrypt's 10 new
 registrations per 3 hours per IP.

fields.name: cert_set_id
fields.description:
cert_set_id identifies the hostname set this certificate covers — a stable
 digest of the sorted, comma-joined Config.hostnames list. Derived, never
 configured: two pods reading the same config must compute the same key.

fields.name: tls_cert
fields.description:
tls_cert is the certificate chain and private key, in the SAME type
 LetsEncryptCertData.tls_cert holds, so the mirror write is a field copy and
 not a conversion.

 NOT assert_required, for the same reason LetsEncryptCertData.tls_cert stopped
 being required in 7ba5060: the FIRST write of this row happens before any
 certificate exists. certmagic registers the ACME account minutes before
 issuance completes, and that account has to become durable at once — Let's
 Encrypt allows 10 new registrations per 3 hours per IP, which a crash-loop
 that re-registers on every boot exhausts. So the account flush writes this
 row with certmagic_state and no tls_cert, and the obtain fills it in. A row
 with no tls_cert means "the account is durable, the certificate is not yet".

message.name: X509CertChain
message.description:
X509CertChain contains a certificate chain and optional private key.
 chain[0] is the leaf (end-entity) cert, followed by intermediates, ordered toward root.
 When key is present, the chain is a full credential suitable for TLS.

fields.name: chain
fields.description: chain[0] is the leaf (end-entity) cert, followed by intermediates, ordered toward root.

message.name: X509Cert
message.description:

 Use NewProtoCert() in Go with DER-encoded certificate bytes to create.

fields.name: base64

fields.name: key

message.description: Key represents a private cryptographic key (alias for ProtoKey).

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is a unique identifier for the key (corresponds to kid in JWK)

fields.name: base64
fields.description: Base64 contains the base64url-encoded PEM private key block

fields.name: created
fields.description:

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is an optional stable key for chain collections.

message.name: CertMagicState
message.description:

fields.name: hostnames
fields.description:
hostnames are the names the certificate was issued for, in the sorted order
 cert_set_id was computed over. Carried as well as digested because a digest

fields.name: issued_at
fields.description:

 is no field here duplicating one there.

fields.name: expires_at
fields.description: expires_at is the leaf certificate's NotAfter, Unix seconds. See issued_at.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record's owner — letsencrypt's own workload identity, the
 only writer this record has.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning namespace — the generated tenant backstop.
 A cluster's TLS certificate is platform data, so this is root ("/") in
 practice; the annotation is mandatory on every record regardless.

 SERVICE's own, not any user it might be acting for.

rpcs.description:
BrokerToolCallback — the caller's reverse MCP binding (A29, BQ1/BQ2; the
 design record's OpenToolCallback, renamed because "Open" is not in tacplus's
 closed verb registry and "Broker" is the verb of the synthesized
 Broker<Service>McpSession carriers this mirrors). The caller opens it; this service SENDS mcp.McpRequest frames (tools/call) and
 RECEIVES mcp.McpResponse frames. One stream per caller SPIFFE identity,
 shared by every thread of that caller; a re-open replaces the old stream
 (latest wins). Identity is the stream's authenticated caller, never anything
 in a frame.

types.name: Config
types.description: Config is delivered by kernel at startup and on every change.

fields.name: api_key_hint_chars
fields.description:
api_key_hint_chars is how many trailing characters of a stored key the read
 surface may echo back, so a person can tell WHICH key is saved without the
 key being retrievable. Config rather than a constant because it is a
 privacy/usability trade a deployment makes, and moving it must not need a
 redeploy. 0 disables the hint entirely.

 Capped at 8: a hint long enough to be searched for is not a hint.

types.name: EventBusRecordMeta
ListMyLlmSettingsRequest

fields.name: owner
fields.description:
owner is (spec.principal): the generated wrapper resolves the authenticated
 caller's subject and stamps it when empty, accepts it when it matches, and
 refuses with INVALID_ARGUMENT when it differs. A caller therefore cannot
 read someone else's settings, and the handler does not check.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is (spec.namespace): the same stamp/accept/refuse control on the
 caller's tenant claim. Declared on a READ, like mailbox.ListHeldMailRequest
 and for the same reason: this handler selects a row out of the record store by
 key rather than handing a list to the egress filter, and it needs the
 caller's verified tenant to check the row against.

 Necessary rather than belt-and-braces: llmsettings reads the record plane's
 S2S half as a `/system` peer, and that plane deliberately leaves a /system
 peer's read UNPINNED — fleet-wide, across tenants (javaNamespaceResolve's
 runtime gate). The tenant narrowing on this path is therefore this handler's
 to apply, and the crashing (spec.store_namespace) egress backstop is what
 catches it getting that wrong.

types.name: ListMyLlmSettingsResponse

fields.name: settings
fields.description:
settings is 0 or 1 rows. Bounded at 1 because more than one settings row
 for one principal is not a large response, it is a broken store.

message.name: LlmProviderSettings
message.description:
LlmProviderSettings is ONE person's LLM API settings, MINUS the key. It is both
 the stored record and the read response's item type, deliberately:
 `(spec.store_principal)` and `(spec.store_namespace)` filter repeated fields OF
 THIS TYPE on the way out, so a bespoke response row would be a read path with
 the generated backstops switched off (mailbox.ListHeldMailResponse says the
 same thing).

 Returning the stored type is safe because the secret is NOT IN IT: the key is
 LlmProviderSecret's, and that type is the item of no rpc on this service. Until
 2026-09-27 the key was field 3 here, made safe by `(spec.redact)` =
 REDACT_MODE_DROP; see the file header for why that annotation and a stratum
 record cannot both hold a secret this service has to read back.

fields.name: owner
fields.description:
owner is the record key AND the row's owning principal.

 (spec.indexed) makes it the record's key, so there is exactly one row per
 person by construction rather than by a uniqueness check somebody has to
 remember to write. (spec.store_principal) is what holds a caller's reads to
 their own row: the generated wrapper filters every repeated
 LlmProviderSettings field in a response down to rows the caller owns, so the
 handler does not check and there is nothing left for it to get wrong.

 spiffe_id below is the record's declared owner but is the PUBLISHER —
 llmsettings' own service identity, stamped by eventbus — so it is the wrong
 field to filter a person's reads on, exactly as it is on mailbox.MailboxEntry.

fields.name: endpoint_url
fields.description:
endpoint_url is the LLM API base URL.

 HTTPS ONLY, and that is not tidiness: this field's companion is a bearer
 secret, and the service that eventually calls this endpoint would put that
 secret in an Authorization header. Permitting http:// here would let a
 person configure their own key's exfiltration. (spec.assert_url) is the
 generated check — nothing in the handler parses a URL.
constraints: must be a valid URL (scheme: URL_SCHEME_HTTPS)

fields.name: api_key_set
fields.description:
api_key_set says whether a key is stored, and exists because the key is not
 in this message at all — a caller reading these rows cannot tell an unset
 key from an absent one without being told. Maintained by the handler on
 write, from the secret row it just published.

 It is what lets the form render "a key is saved — replace it?" rather than
 an empty box that silently means either thing.

fields.name: api_key_hint
fields.description:
api_key_hint is the last Config.api_key_hint_chars characters of the stored
 key, so a person with several keys can tell WHICH one is saved. Not
 redacted: it is a deliberate, bounded disclosure, and the bound is the
 config knob rather than this field's own max_size so that lowering the knob
 takes effect on the next write instead of needing a proto change.

 8 is the ceiling Config.api_key_hint_chars enforces; this bound restates it
 so an oversized value is rejected by generated validation even if a future
 handler computes it wrong.

fields.name: updated_at_ms
fields.description: updated_at_ms is when the row was last written. Server-assigned.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT, by exact string equality against the
 reader's namespace claim. MANDATORY on a record: tacplus fails generation for
 any (spec.record) declaring no such field, on the reasoning that the record
 nobody remembered to annotate is exactly the one that leaks.
 (spec.store_namespace) generates the read-side egress filter on every surface
 returning this row; the write half is UpdateLlmSettingsRequest.namespace's
 (spec.namespace).

 Not a query field: the field exists to BE the egress boundary, and a boundary
 a caller can predicate on is not one. The handler compares it itself on the
 record-plane read, because that plane leaves a `/system` peer's read
 deliberately unpinned — see ListMyLlmSettingsRequest.namespace.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner, and the name is LOAD-BEARING: eventbus's topic
 discovery matches the LITERAL field name "spiffe_id" of string type when it
 decides which topics get publisher-identity stamping, so renaming it silently
 turns the stamping off.

 It holds LLMSETTINGS' OWN service identity — this service is the publisher.
 `owner` above is where the person is.

types.name: LlmProviderSecret
types.description:
LlmProviderSecret is ONE person's LLM API key, in a record that NO CLIENT-FACING
 RPC RETURNS. That absence is the whole protection, and it is stronger than the
 `(spec.redact)` it replaced: a redaction is a transform that must run on every
 egress path, whereas a type absent from every response message has no egress
 path to run on. Nothing on `service LlmSettings` names this type — check that
 before adding an rpc, because adding one is the only way to undo it.

 It is letsencrypt.LetsEncryptCert's posture applied to the same class of
 secret: a cluster TLS private key lives unredacted in a stratum record whose
 readers are named by `s2s_read`, because a service that has to USE a secret
 has to be able to read it, and the grant list is what bounds who else can.

 SEPARATE ROW, SAME KEY. Keyed by the same `owner` as LlmProviderSettings, so
 the pair is joinable by identity and there is no second id to keep in step. The
 two are written in one operation and NOT atomically — records have no
 multi-row write — so the handler publishes THIS row first: `api_key_set` on the
 settings row must never claim a key that is not yet durable. The reverse order
 would advertise a key that a crash could lose.

fields.name: owner
fields.description:
owner is the record key and the row's owning principal — the same person, and
 the same value, as LlmProviderSettings.owner.

fields.name: api_key
fields.description:
api_key is the secret, stored as given.

 NOT (spec.redact), and that is the point of this message existing rather than
 an omission: DROP would clear the field on the record plane's own read and
 leave this service unable to read back the key it wrote (file header). What
 keeps it safe is that no response message anywhere carries this type.

 Not a (spec.query_field) either, on top of the general rule that a filterable
 secret is a guessing oracle: nothing queries by key value, and the point read
 on `owner` is the only access this row has.

fields.name: updated_at_ms
fields.description:
updated_at_ms is when this row was last written. Server-assigned, and the
 same clock value the settings row carries for the same save, so a pair that
 disagrees is a partially-applied write rather than two independent ones.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT — mandatory on every record, and copied
 from the same verified caller claim the settings row is stamped from.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner: llmsettings' own service identity, stamped by
 eventbus. The literal name is load-bearing — see
 LlmProviderSettings.spiffe_id.

types.name: LlmProviderSettings
types.description:
LlmProviderSettings is ONE person's LLM API settings, MINUS the key. It is both
 the stored record and the read response's item type, deliberately:
 `(spec.store_principal)` and `(spec.store_namespace)` filter repeated fields OF
 THIS TYPE on the way out, so a bespoke response row would be a read path with
 the generated backstops switched off (mailbox.ListHeldMailResponse says the
 same thing).

 Returning the stored type is safe because the secret is NOT IN IT: the key is
 LlmProviderSecret's, and that type is the item of no rpc on this service. Until
 2026-09-27 the key was field 3 here, made safe by `(spec.redact)` =
 REDACT_MODE_DROP; see the file header for why that annotation and a stratum
 record cannot both hold a secret this service has to read back.

fields.name: owner
fields.description:
owner is the record key AND the row's owning principal.

 (spec.indexed) makes it the record's key, so there is exactly one row per
 person by construction rather than by a uniqueness check somebody has to
 remember to write. (spec.store_principal) is what holds a caller's reads to
 their own row: the generated wrapper filters every repeated
 LlmProviderSettings field in a response down to rows the caller owns, so the
 handler does not check and there is nothing left for it to get wrong.

 spiffe_id below is the record's declared owner but is the PUBLISHER —
 llmsettings' own service identity, stamped by eventbus — so it is the wrong
 field to filter a person's reads on, exactly as it is on mailbox.MailboxEntry.

fields.name: endpoint_url
fields.description:
endpoint_url is the LLM API base URL.

 HTTPS ONLY, and that is not tidiness: this field's companion is a bearer
 secret, and the service that eventually calls this endpoint would put that
 secret in an Authorization header. Permitting http:// here would let a
 person configure their own key's exfiltration. (spec.assert_url) is the
 generated check — nothing in the handler parses a URL.
constraints: must be a valid URL (scheme: URL_SCHEME_HTTPS)

fields.name: api_key_set
fields.description:
api_key_set says whether a key is stored, and exists because the key is not
 in this message at all — a caller reading these rows cannot tell an unset
 key from an absent one without being told. Maintained by the handler on
 write, from the secret row it just published.

 It is what lets the form render "a key is saved — replace it?" rather than
 an empty box that silently means either thing.

fields.name: api_key_hint
fields.description:
api_key_hint is the last Config.api_key_hint_chars characters of the stored
 key, so a person with several keys can tell WHICH one is saved. Not
 redacted: it is a deliberate, bounded disclosure, and the bound is the
 config knob rather than this field's own max_size so that lowering the knob
 takes effect on the next write instead of needing a proto change.

 8 is the ceiling Config.api_key_hint_chars enforces; this bound restates it
 so an oversized value is rejected by generated validation even if a future
 handler computes it wrong.

fields.name: updated_at_ms
fields.description: updated_at_ms is when the row was last written. Server-assigned.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT, by exact string equality against the
 reader's namespace claim. MANDATORY on a record: tacplus fails generation for
 any (spec.record) declaring no such field, on the reasoning that the record
 nobody remembered to annotate is exactly the one that leaks.
 (spec.store_namespace) generates the read-side egress filter on every surface
 returning this row; the write half is UpdateLlmSettingsRequest.namespace's
 (spec.namespace).

 Not a query field: the field exists to BE the egress boundary, and a boundary
 a caller can predicate on is not one. The handler compares it itself on the
 record-plane read, because that plane leaves a `/system` peer's read
 deliberately unpinned — see ListMyLlmSettingsRequest.namespace.
