LlmsettingsConfigState is the state boundary for llmsettings service configuration.
 Auto-injected by tacplus from (spec.grpc_config) annotation.

message.name: Config
message.description: Config is delivered by kernel at startup and on every change.

fields.name: api_key_hint_chars
fields.description:
api_key_hint_chars is how many trailing characters of a stored key the read
 surface may echo back, so a person can tell WHICH key is saved without the
 key being retrievable. Config rather than a constant because it is a
 privacy/usability trade a deployment makes, and moving it must not need a
 redeploy. 0 disables the hint entirely.

 Capped at 8: a hint long enough to be searched for is not a hint.

types.name: MapEmpty
UpdateLlmSettingsRequest

fields.name: owner
fields.description:
owner is (spec.principal) — see ListMyLlmSettingsRequest. It is what makes
 "save MY settings" unable to name anybody else's row, before the handler
 runs.

fields.name: endpoint_url
fields.description:
endpoint_url is required on every save: it is the half of the settings that
 is not a secret, so there is no "leave it alone" case to represent — a
 caller that wants it unchanged sends back what it just read.
constraints: must be a valid URL (scheme: URL_SCHEME_HTTPS)

fields.name: api_key
fields.description:
api_key is OPTIONAL on a save, and empty means LEAVE THE STORED KEY ALONE.

 That asymmetry with endpoint_url is forced by the key being unreadable by
 clients: a client never holds the current key, so it cannot send it back
 unchanged the way it can an endpoint. Empty therefore has to mean "no
 change" — the alternative, clearing on empty, would delete a person's key
 every time they edited only the URL.

 This is the one requirement that decided the shape of the storage: honouring
 it means the SERVICE must be able to read the stored key, which is why the
 key lives in LlmProviderSecret (readable by llmsettings over `s2s_read`)
 rather than in a `(spec.redact)`-DROP field the record plane would hand back
 empty. See the file header.

 Removing a key is consequently not something this RPC can express. Nothing
 needs it yet, and inventing a clear_api_key flag before something does
 would be inventing product; see questions.md.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is (spec.namespace) — the write half of the tenant pair. This RPC
 writes rows, so the marker is doing its primary job here: binding the value
 the handler then stamps onto BOTH rows' namespace, and compares the rows it
 reads back against.

types.name: UpdateLlmSettingsResponse

fields.name: updated_at_ms
fields.description:
updated_at_ms is the timestamp the saved row now carries.

 The row itself is NOT echoed back. A singular `LlmProviderSettings settings` field
 here would be the shape the (spec.store_namespace) egress backstop skips —
 it is generated only for repeated fields — so echoing one would be the one
 response in this file with the tenant filter switched off. The client
 re-reads through ListMyLlmSettings, which has it — and can do so immediately,
 because this rpc does not return until the row it wrote is visible.

rpcs.description:
ListMyLlmSettings returns the calling principal's own LLM settings: zero
 rows when nothing has been saved, one when something has. The api_key is
 never among them — it is not a field of the type this returns.

 Served by a point read of the LlmProviderSettings record on `owner`, over the
 record plane's S2S half. There is no cache and no kernel copy in front of it:
 a settings form saves and immediately re-reads, and answering that re-read
 from anything but the store would show the person their OLD endpoint and make
 the save look like it failed. The save is what waits for visibility (see
 UpdateLlmSettings), so by the time a client can issue this read the row it
 wants is there.

 LIST, NOT GET, and the verb is not a style choice. The response carries a
 repeated field, tacplus classifies that as a collection read, and its
 closed verb registry refuses a collection read spelled Get. The response is
 repeated in the first place because that is the only shape the
 (spec.store_namespace) egress backstop is generated for — it skips any
 field that is not repeated, so a singular `LlmProviderSettings settings` would
 carry the annotation and generate no backstop at all, silently. Same
 finding as scottyagent.ListMyAgentStateResponse.
rpcs.verb_definition: Finite/paginated set, ordered by order_by; filters are fields.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Get-plural/Search/Query; collection reads must declare method_collection.

rpcs.description:
UpdateLlmSettings saves the caller's endpoint and, when one is supplied, a
 new API key.

 IT ACKS ON VISIBILITY, not on publish. A record's write path is a publish
 onto its topic and stratum's ingest of that topic, which is asynchronous —
 so after publishing, this rpc point-reads the row back until it sees its own
 `updated_at_ms`, bounded to the sub-second window that hop takes, and only
 then returns. That is what makes the client's immediate `ListMyLlmSettings`
 correct without kernel state behind it (Jody, 2026-09-27). A timeout is
 reported as a failure of the SAVE rather than swallowed: the publish will
 still land, but a client told "saved" and then shown the old row is the one
 outcome this must not produce.

 TWO ROWS, SECRET FIRST: see LlmProviderSecret. Not atomic, and ordered so
 that the failure mode is a durable key nothing points at rather than an
 `api_key_set` pointing at nothing.

 Update rather than Create, and there is no Create: a person's settings row
 is upsert-shaped — the first save and the fifth are the same operation, and
 a Create/Update pair would make the client ask "does my row exist yet"
 before it could save. `Set` is a registered synonym of Update, so this is
 the canonical spelling of that verb.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Merge; changes one existing resource rather than combining resources.

rpcs.description:
BrokerLlmSettingsMcpSession carries one Model Context Protocol session for LlmSettings over a
 single bidirectional stream: one complete JSON-RPC frame per stream message,
 request frames in and response frames out, for the life of the session.

 Generated, never declared: LlmSettings has at least one RPC_PRINCIPAL_MCP rpc, and this
 is the only channel those tools are reachable through. Bidirectional because an
 MCP session is stateful — it opens with an initialize handshake and holds the
 negotiated protocol version after it — so a unary call would repeat that
 handshake per tool call.
rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

services.name: LlmSettings
services.description:
LlmSettings is user-facing: it accepts user tokens minted from a browser
 login. There is no s2s read surface on it yet, and that is not an oversight —
 nothing calls an LLM in this fleet today. The service that eventually does
 declares `(spec.grpc_s2s_client)` for it and this file grows one s2s rpc.

types.name: Config
types.description: Config is delivered by kernel at startup and on every change.

fields.name: sweep_interval_seconds
fields.description:
sweep_interval_seconds is INERT as of 2026-09-27 and is read by nothing.

 It was the cadence of the STATE-ROOT sweep: `MailboxState.entries` was this
 service's own root in kernel, nothing else pruned it, and an unbounded one
 eventually reached its declared 1,000,000 bound and started refusing
 writes. There is no such root any more — the rows live in stratum, whose
 bound is disk and whose memory clock is `residency.idle_seconds` below, a
 per-type clock this service can neither observe nor set. A sweep from here
 would have nothing to sweep.

 WHAT WENT WITH IT: the 90-day `held_since_ms` floor. That age was the STATE
 ROOT's bound, not the record's, and no record-side clock replaces it —
 `residency.deleted_max_age_seconds` measures a purge from a
 `(spec.deleted_flag)` this record does not declare. So a mailbox entry is
 now kept for as long as stratum keeps it. See held_since_ms's comment and
 workers/mailbox-llmsettings-stratum-result.md; deliberately NOT closed here
 by inventing a delete path this migration was not asked for.

 (Until 2026-09-20 the sweep had a second half, reconciling the retired
 `ejectionable` marker. That half went first; this is the rest.)

 kernel holds mailbox's config, and removing a field kernel sets is a
 config-compatibility question this migration has no answer for. Both should
 be deleted and fields 1 and 2 reserved in a follow-up once nothing in kernel
 sets either.

fields.name: retrieved_grace_seconds
fields.description:
retrieved_grace_seconds is INERT as of 2026-09-20 and is read by nothing.

 It had exactly one job: to defer the moment the sweep flipped a retrieved
 row's `ejectionable` from NEVER to WINDOW, so that a client which acks and
 then immediately re-reads still found the row resident. Both ends of that
 sentence are gone. The marker went with `spec.Ejectionable`, and residency
 is now a per-TYPE idle clock on the row's last touch — a grace period
 cannot shift it, because the retrieval write IS the touch.

 DECLARED, not deleted, on purpose: kernel holds mailbox's config, and
 removing the field is a config-compatibility question this migration has no
 answer for. It should be deleted and field 2 reserved in a follow-up once
 nothing in kernel sets it — see
 looper/schematic/workers/mailbox-ejectionable-migration-questions.md. The
 same now applies to sweep_interval_seconds above.

types.name: EventBusRecordMeta
ListHeldMailRequest

fields.name: recipient
fields.description:
recipient is (spec.principal): the generated wrapper resolves the
 authenticated caller's subject and stamps it when empty, accepts it when it
 matches, and refuses with INVALID_ARGUMENT when it differs. A caller
 therefore cannot read someone else's mailbox, and the handler does not
 check — there is nothing left to check.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is (spec.namespace): the same stamp/accept/refuse control on the
 caller's tenant claim. It is declared on a READ here, unlike scotty's MCP
 audit rpc which omits it, because this handler does not merely return rows
 for the generated egress filter to police — it selects them out of the
 record store by predicate, and the predicate needs the caller's verified
 tenant. Necessary rather than belt-and-braces: mailbox reads the record
 plane's S2S half as a `/system` peer, which that plane deliberately leaves
 UNPINNED (a fleet-wide read, see javaNamespaceResolve's runtime gate), so
 the tenant narrowing on this path is this handler's to apply.

types.name: ListHeldMailResponse

fields.name: entries
fields.description:
The held entries, newest arrival last. Carrying the record type rather than
 a hand-rolled summary struct is deliberate: `(spec.store_principal)` and
 `(spec.store_namespace)` filter repeated fields OF THAT RECORD TYPE on the
 way out, so a bespoke response row would be a read path with the generated
 backstop switched off.

message.name: MailboxEntry
message.description:
MailboxEntry is ONE DELIVERY'S mailbox state, keyed by the SAME delivery_id
 as the `messaging.Message` it tracks.

 Joinable by identity, not by a second lookup: an entry and its message share
 a key, so "fetch the body of the mail I was just told about" is one Message
 read with an id the client already holds.

 IT HOLDS NO BODY. `messaging.Message.text` is never copied here — that is the
 decision doc's rejected alternative ("Mailbox stores full message content"),
 and it stands. What IS carried is the inbox SUMMARY LINE the doc's own
 ListHeldMail spec enumerates (sender, subject, sent_at_ms): a mail client
 renders a list before anything is opened, and those three fields are the only
 way to serve that list without a second round trip per row. A summary line is
 not a second copy of the message, and the field that would make it one —
 `text` — is absent, as are `recipients` and `ticket_id`.

fields.name: delivery_id
fields.description:
delivery_id is the record key and messaging.Message.delivery_id verbatim.
 Bounded identically (512) — a shorter bound here would silently drop the
 deliveries whose recipient subject is long.

fields.name: message_id
fields.description:
message_id groups the N entries of one submission, the same way it groups
 the N Messages. EQ-filterable for the same reason it is there.

fields.name: recipient
fields.description:
recipient is whose mailbox this is, and the ROW'S OWNING PRINCIPAL — the
 same field, carrying the same annotation, as messaging.Message.recipient.
 The generated egress filter holds a caller's reads to their own rows, so
 ListHeldMail cannot return one person's mail to another even if this
 service's own predicate were wrong.

 spiffe_id below is the record's declared owner but is the PUBLISHER —
 mailbox's own service identity, stamped by eventbus — so it is the wrong
 field to filter a user's reads on, exactly as it is on Message.

enum_values.name: MAILBOX_ENTRY_STATUS_HELD
enum_values.description:
HELD: the delivery arrived on the topic and nobody has pulled it. Age alone
 does not change that, and no longer needs a marker to say so: an unpulled
 row may leave the store's MEMORY like any other and loses nothing by it —
 it stays complete and queryable on disk, and the next read reloads it.
 NOTHING removes a HELD row: the 90-day `held_since_ms` floor that used to
 was the kernel state root's bound, and the root went away with it on
 2026-09-27 — see Config.sweep_interval_seconds.

enum_values.name: MAILBOX_ENTRY_STATUS_RETRIEVED
enum_values.description:
RETRIEVED: the recipient acknowledged pulling it. Terminal in the normal
 path — `ListHeldMail` stops returning the row and `UpdateHeldMail` is a
 no-op on it — so this is the row's last write, and therefore where its
 residency idle clock starts running down.

fields.name: held_since_ms
fields.description:
held_since_ms is when this consumer group's copy landed. It is NOT a
 residency clock — residency runs on the row's last touch, which is
 store_epoch_ms and is the store's business, not a business field's. It is
 not an expiry clock either, as of 2026-09-27: the state-root sweep it used
 to drive is gone with the state root, and no record-side clock replaced it
 (see Config.sweep_interval_seconds). What survives is the question a user
 asks with it — "how long has this been sitting in my mailbox" — and the
 ordering `ListHeldMail` presents.

 RANGE-filterable because "what has been sitting in my mailbox since last
 week" is a question about this field.

fields.name: retrieved_at_ms
fields.description:
retrieved_at_ms is unset until retrieved: when the recipient took it, which
 is what a read inbox sorts by and what UpdateHeldMail's idempotency is
 stated in terms of (the FIRST retrieval's timestamp stands).

 It gates nothing in this service any more. Until 2026-09-20 it was the
 clock the eviction-eligibility mark was measured from; that mark went with
 `ejectionable`, and the residency clock that replaced it counts from the
 row's last WRITE — which, for a retrieved row, is the retrieval itself. The
 field survives because "when did I take this" is the user's question and
 does not stop being worth answering.

fields.name: sender
fields.description:
sender is messaging.Message.sender — the authenticated principal that sent
 it, never a caller-written string on either side.

fields.name: subject
fields.description: subject is the subject line. Bounded identically to Message.subject.

fields.name: sent_at_ms
fields.description:
sent_at_ms is the sender's clock, carried through so an inbox can sort by
 when a message was SENT rather than by when this consumer group happened to
 process it. The two differ by broker latency and by any replay.

fields.name: store_epoch_ms
fields.description:
store_epoch_ms is the row's LAST WRITE, stamped by the generated wrapper
 and never by this service. It is the record's durable write clock: what the
 disk leg ranges on, and what `residency.deleted_max_age_seconds` would
 measure a delete from if this type had a (spec.deleted_flag). The memory
 idle clock also counts READS, which no field can see — which is precisely
 why residency is a property of the type and not of the row.

 RANGE per (spec.store_epoch)'s own contract — it is the predicate a
 two-leg memory/disk query partitions on.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner, and the name is LOAD-BEARING: eventbus's
 topic discovery matches the literal field name "spiffe_id" of string type
 when deciding which topics get publisher-identity stamping.

 It holds MAILBOX'S OWN service identity — this service is the publisher.
 `recipient` above is where the person is.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT, by EXACT string equality against the
 caller's namespace claim. MANDATORY: tacplus fails generation for any
 (spec.record) declaring no such field, on the reasoning that the record
 nobody remembered to annotate is exactly the one that leaks.

 Its value is copied from the Message that produced this entry rather than
 resolved again: the tenant of a mailbox entry IS the tenant of the delivery
 it tracks, and re-deriving it from mailbox's own service token would stamp
 the SERVICE's tenant onto a USER's row.

 Not a (spec.query_field): the field exists to be the egress boundary, and a
 boundary a caller can name in a predicate is not one.

 It holds MAILBOX'S OWN service identity — this service is the publisher.
 `recipient` above is where the person is.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT, by EXACT string equality against the
 caller's namespace claim. MANDATORY: tacplus fails generation for any
 (spec.record) declaring no such field, on the reasoning that the record
 nobody remembered to annotate is exactly the one that leaks.

 Its value is copied from the Message that produced this entry rather than
 resolved again: the tenant of a mailbox entry IS the tenant of the delivery
 it tracks, and re-deriving it from mailbox's own service token would stamp
 the SERVICE's tenant onto a USER's row.

 Not a (spec.query_field): the field exists to be the egress boundary, and a
 boundary a caller can name in a predicate is not one.

types.name: MailboxEntryBusStreamSubscribeRecord

message.name: MailboxEntry
message.description:
MailboxEntry is ONE DELIVERY'S mailbox state, keyed by the SAME delivery_id
 as the `messaging.Message` it tracks.

 Joinable by identity, not by a second lookup: an entry and its message share
 a key, so "fetch the body of the mail I was just told about" is one Message
 read with an id the client already holds.

 IT HOLDS NO BODY. `messaging.Message.text` is never copied here — that is the
 decision doc's rejected alternative ("Mailbox stores full message content"),
 and it stands. What IS carried is the inbox SUMMARY LINE the doc's own
 ListHeldMail spec enumerates (sender, subject, sent_at_ms): a mail client
 renders a list before anything is opened, and those three fields are the only
 way to serve that list without a second round trip per row. A summary line is
 not a second copy of the message, and the field that would make it one —
 `text` — is absent, as are `recipients` and `ticket_id`.

fields.name: delivery_id
fields.description:
delivery_id is the record key and messaging.Message.delivery_id verbatim.
 Bounded identically (512) — a shorter bound here would silently drop the
 deliveries whose recipient subject is long.

fields.name: message_id
fields.description:
message_id groups the N entries of one submission, the same way it groups
 the N Messages. EQ-filterable for the same reason it is there.

fields.name: recipient
fields.description:
recipient is whose mailbox this is, and the ROW'S OWNING PRINCIPAL — the
 same field, carrying the same annotation, as messaging.Message.recipient.
 The generated egress filter holds a caller's reads to their own rows, so
 ListHeldMail cannot return one person's mail to another even if this
 service's own predicate were wrong.

 spiffe_id below is the record's declared owner but is the PUBLISHER —
 mailbox's own service identity, stamped by eventbus — so it is the wrong
 field to filter a user's reads on, exactly as it is on Message.

enum_values.name: MAILBOX_ENTRY_STATUS_HELD
enum_values.description:
HELD: the delivery arrived on the topic and nobody has pulled it. Age alone
 does not change that, and no longer needs a marker to say so: an unpulled
 row may leave the store's MEMORY like any other and loses nothing by it —
 it stays complete and queryable on disk, and the next read reloads it.
 NOTHING removes a HELD row: the 90-day `held_since_ms` floor that used to
 was the kernel state root's bound, and the root went away with it on
 2026-09-27 — see Config.sweep_interval_seconds.

enum_values.name: MAILBOX_ENTRY_STATUS_RETRIEVED
enum_values.description:
RETRIEVED: the recipient acknowledged pulling it. Terminal in the normal
 path — `ListHeldMail` stops returning the row and `UpdateHeldMail` is a
 no-op on it — so this is the row's last write, and therefore where its
 residency idle clock starts running down.

fields.name: held_since_ms
fields.description:
held_since_ms is when this consumer group's copy landed. It is NOT a
 residency clock — residency runs on the row's last touch, which is
 store_epoch_ms and is the store's business, not a business field's. It is
 not an expiry clock either, as of 2026-09-27: the state-root sweep it used
 to drive is gone with the state root, and no record-side clock replaced it
 (see Config.sweep_interval_seconds). What survives is the question a user
 asks with it — "how long has this been sitting in my mailbox" — and the
 ordering `ListHeldMail` presents.

 RANGE-filterable because "what has been sitting in my mailbox since last
 week" is a question about this field.

fields.name: retrieved_at_ms
fields.description:
retrieved_at_ms is unset until retrieved: when the recipient took it, which
 is what a read inbox sorts by and what UpdateHeldMail's idempotency is
 stated in terms of (the FIRST retrieval's timestamp stands).

 It gates nothing in this service any more. Until 2026-09-20 it was the
 clock the eviction-eligibility mark was measured from; that mark went with
 `ejectionable`, and the residency clock that replaced it counts from the
 row's last WRITE — which, for a retrieved row, is the retrieval itself. The
 field survives because "when did I take this" is the user's question and
 does not stop being worth answering.

fields.name: sender
fields.description:
sender is messaging.Message.sender — the authenticated principal that sent
 it, never a caller-written string on either side.

fields.name: subject
fields.description: subject is the subject line. Bounded identically to Message.subject.

fields.name: sent_at_ms
fields.description:
sent_at_ms is the sender's clock, carried through so an inbox can sort by
 when a message was SENT rather than by when this consumer group happened to
 process it. The two differ by broker latency and by any replay.

fields.name: store_epoch_ms
fields.description:
store_epoch_ms is the row's LAST WRITE, stamped by the generated wrapper
 and never by this service. It is the record's durable write clock: what the
 disk leg ranges on, and what `residency.deleted_max_age_seconds` would
 measure a delete from if this type had a (spec.deleted_flag). The memory
 idle clock also counts READS, which no field can see — which is precisely
 why residency is a property of the type and not of the row.

 RANGE per (spec.store_epoch)'s own contract — it is the predicate a
 two-leg memory/disk query partitions on.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner, and the name is LOAD-BEARING: eventbus's
 topic discovery matches the literal field name "spiffe_id" of string type

 It holds MAILBOX'S OWN service identity — this service is the publisher.
 `recipient` above is where the person is.

fields.name: recipient
fields.description:
recipient is (spec.principal) — see ListHeldMailRequest. It is what makes
 "retrieve MY mail" unable to name anybody else's delivery, before the

fields.name: delivery_ids
fields.description:
delivery_ids are the deliveries being acknowledged. Bounded to the page

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is (spec.namespace) — the write half of the tenant pair. This RPC

 the handler then holds a row's own stamped namespace against.

types.name: UpdateHeldMailResponse

fields.name: retrieved_delivery_ids
fields.description:
retrieved_delivery_ids is what this call actually changed from HELD to
 RETRIEVED — a SUBSET of the request's ids, and the difference is the point.
 An id that was already retrieved, or that names no entry of the caller's,
 is absent here rather than an error, so a client can tell "I acked this
 just now" from "this was already acked" without either being a failure.

fields.name: retrieved_at_ms
fields.description:
retrieved_at_ms is the timestamp stamped on the entries this call retrieved
 — one clock for the call, the same way messaging takes one sent_at_ms for a
 whole submission. Zero when the call retrieved nothing.

rpcs.description:
ListHeldMail returns the deliveries still HELD for the calling recipient.

 It is the "do I have new mail" poll, and it returns no message body — only
 enough to know what to fetch from messaging. See MailboxEntry's comment.
rpcs.verb_definition: Finite/paginated set, ordered by order_by; filters are fields.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Get-plural/Search/Query; collection reads must declare method_collection.

rpcs.description:
UpdateHeldMail marks deliveries RETRIEVED, which is what takes them out of
 `ListHeldMail`'s answer.

 NOT `RetrieveMail`, which is what the decision doc calls it. The RPC verb
 registry is CLOSED (tacplus/pkg/internal/common/verbs/registry.json) and
 `Retrieve` is neither a registered verb nor a folded synonym of one, so
 that name does not generate at all — verbs.Classify hard-fails any c2s
 method whose leading verb is unregistered. This is the same trap item 5 hit
 with `Submit` (resolved there to `Send`). `Update` is the registered verb
 whose definition is this operation — "modify an existing resource" — and
 the rows it modifies are the ones `ListHeldMail` just returned, so the pair
 reads as one noun with two verbs. Nothing about the semantics the doc
 settled changes: the operation, its idempotency and its effect on
 `retrieved_at_ms` are exactly as specified there.

 IDEMPOTENT. Naming an id that is already RETRIEVED is a no-op, not an
 error: a client polling on reconnect must not fail on ids it already acked,
 and the FIRST retrieval's timestamp is the one that stands — a second call
 must not rewrite when the recipient took the mail.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Merge; changes one existing resource rather than combining resources.

rpcs.description:
BrokerMailboxMcpSession carries one Model Context Protocol session for Mailbox over a
 single bidirectional stream: one complete JSON-RPC frame per stream message,
 request frames in and response frames out, for the life of the session.

 Generated, never declared: Mailbox has at least one RPC_PRINCIPAL_MCP rpc, and this
 is the only channel those tools are reachable through. Bidirectional because an
 MCP session is stateful — it opens with an initialize handshake and holds the
 negotiated protocol version after it — so a unary call would repeat that
 handshake per tool call.
rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

types.name: AgentReceivedReceipt
types.description:
AgentReceivedReceipt is the delivery ACK — the agent (scotty, the mailbox
 service) took the record off the topic and processed it. Written by the
 consumer, never by the sender or by this service.

 It is the ACK, not a copy of it: there is one event here, not a delivery ACK
 plus a receipt derived from it.

fields.name: received_at_ms
fields.description:
received_at_ms is when the consuming agent completed processing — the same
 instant it commits its consumer-group offset, since committing before
 processing is exactly the discipline the queue semantics forbid.

fields.name: received_by
fields.description: received_by is the SPIFFE identity of the consuming agent instance.

types.name: Config
types.description: Config is delivered by kernel at startup and on every change.

fields.name: max_recipients
fields.description:
max_recipients bounds the recipient fan-out of ONE submission, and it is a
 resource limit on the service, not a business rule: N recipients means N
 publishes, so an unbounded list is an unbounded amount of work bought with
 one RPC. Held in config rather than as a constant for the same reason
 tasks.Config.max_open_tasks is — changing it in kernel must change
 behaviour with no redeploy.

 It must not exceed SendMessageRequest.recipients' assert_max_size (256):
 the two describe the same cap and the generated request validation is the
 hard edge, so a config above it could never take effect.

types.name: EventBusRecordMeta
HumanViewedReceipt
types.description:
HumanViewedReceipt fires when the actual person looked at the message. A
 distinct signal from AgentReceivedReceipt above: an agent can have ACKed a
 message hours before a human sees it, and business-hours-deferred
 presentation makes that gap the normal case rather than the exception.

 Presentation is a passive pull label — the reader is told "viewed", never
 pushed a notification. That is the design already built for tickets
 (decisions/ticket-read-receipts-2026-08-30.md), relocated to where it
 belongs.

fields.name: viewed_at_ms
fields.description: viewed_at_ms is when the person actually looked.

fields.name: viewed_by
fields.description:
viewed_by is the principal subject of the person who looked. It is normally
 equal to Message.recipient — a delivery is viewed by its addressee — but it
 is stored rather than assumed, because a delegate viewing on someone's
 behalf is a real case and an inferred value could not tell the two apart.

types.name: MapEmpty
Message
types.description:
Message is ONE DELIVERY: one message, to one recipient.

 It is NOT one row per submission. A submission naming three recipients
 becomes three `Message` rows sharing a `message_id`, differing in
 `delivery_id` and `recipient`, each independently consumable and
 independently ACKable. See the fan-out note at the top of this file for why
 EventBus cannot do that split itself.

 spec.record implies spec.event, so tacplus synthesizes the topic wrapper
 MessageBus with topic ref messaging.MessageBus.stream. Do NOT hand-write that
 wrapper.

fields.name: delivery_id
fields.description:
delivery_id is the record key: "<message_id>/<recipient>". One per
 (message, recipient) pair, which is what makes the N publishes of one
 submission N separately-keyed records rather than N copies of one.

 Derived rather than random ON PURPOSE: the value a caller would need to
 reconstruct to ACK a delivery is exactly (which message, for whom), so
 deriving it means an agent that knows both never has to have been told the
 id. It is also what makes the fan-out replay-safe — a retried submission
 regenerates the same delivery ids rather than a second set of rows.

fields.name: message_id
fields.description:
message_id groups the N deliveries of ONE submission. EQ-filterable,
 because "every delivery of the message I sent" is the question a sender
 asks, and it is the only way back from a delivery to its siblings.

fields.name: sender
fields.description:
sender is who sent it — the authenticated principal subject bound by the
 (spec.principal) field on SendMessageRequest below, never a caller-written
 string.

fields.name: recipient
fields.description:
recipient is THE recipient this delivery is for — one of `recipients`
 below, and the half of delivery_id that varies across the fan-out.

 It is also the ROW'S OWNING PRINCIPAL for the record query plane's c2s
 half. spiffe_id below is the record's declared owner but is the PUBLISHER —
 eventbus stamps messaging's own service identity onto it — so filtering a
 user's reads on that field would show every user nothing. `sender` is the
 other candidate and is the wrong one: a mailbox read is "messages addressed
 to me", so the field the generated egress filter holds a caller's reads to
 must be the addressee.

 The consequence is stated rather than hidden: a SENDER cannot read their own
 sent messages through this record's c2s plane, because only one field may
 carry (spec.store_principal) and this is it. Sent-items is a mailbox
 concern and the mailbox service is Phase 1 item 8, undesigned; inventing a
 second read path for it here would be inventing that service's shape.

 The EQ criterion is what carries the row filter into the plane's SIZE-ONLY
 RPCs: Get<T>Count returns a number over the handle's predicate and no rows,
 so no egress filter can narrow it. The generated c2s wrapper pins this
 criterion to the caller at Create<T>Query and every later call on the
 handle inherits it.

fields.name: recipients
fields.description:
recipients is the full To: line — every recipient of the submission, the
 SAME list on all N deliveries. `recipient` above says which one this row is
 for; this says who else got it.

 Carrying it is not redundancy. Without it a recipient cannot see who else
 was addressed, which is information the sender chose to disclose by
 addressing them together — the same reason a To: header exists and a Bcc:
 one does not. (This file models no Bcc; nothing has asked for one.)

 Bounded at 256 to match Config.max_recipients' ceiling above.

fields.name: subject
fields.description: subject is the message's subject line.

fields.name: text
fields.description: text is the message body. Free text, and nothing parses it — see ticket_id.

fields.name: ticket_id
fields.description:
ticket_id OPTIONALLY references the ticket this message pertains to.

 A dedicated field, never a value embedded in `text`. Routing and status
 display have to associate a message with its ticket to act, and the
 standing rule is that anything that must be parsed to be acted on should
 have been a field. Optional because most messages pertain to no ticket, and
 EQ-filterable because "every message about this ticket" is the question the
 field exists to answer.

 This is the ONLY ticket-shaped thing on Message, and it is an opaque id.
 Ticket's own churn — advice sealing, decision chains, amend/reconsider —
 stays entirely inside Ticket. That is what keeps this type stable.

fields.name: sent_at_ms
fields.description:
sent_at_ms is the business clock — when the sender submitted — and the
 RANGE criterion, because "my messages from last week" is the question a
 mailbox asks.

 Identical across all N deliveries of one submission: they were one act.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner. The name is LOAD-BEARING: eventbus's topic
 discovery matches the literal field name "spiffe_id" of string type when it
 decides which topics get publisher-identity stamping, so renaming this
 field silently turns the stamping off.

 It holds MESSAGING'S OWN service identity, not the sender's, because the
 publish is s2s from this service — that is the direct consequence of the
 SUPERSEDED ruling. `sender` above is where the human is.

fields.name: spiffe_actor
fields.description:
spiffe_actor is the ORIGIN signal: the delegate that made the call, stamped
 by EventBus from the publishing token's `act` claim at publish time.

   "a message is marked as originating from the user directly or from the
    user's Scotty acting on their behalf... A message sent by
    Scotty-for-Dennis carries `act` populated; one Dennis sends directly
    doesn't." — decisions/messaging-vs-ticketing-2026-08-31.md

 The service does not set it and must not: like spiffe_id above, a value
 written here would be a claim about identity that nothing verified.
 Provenance only — sys/spec.proto forbids wiring it into a principal.

 GAP, STATED NOT PAPERED OVER. That quote describes the pre-supersession
 model, where the user published to EventBus DIRECTLY and EventBus saw the
 user's own delegated token. Under the corrected model the publish is s2s
 from messaging, so the token EventBus stamps from is messaging's own
 service token and carries no `act` claim at all — this field will be empty
 in the ordinary case, including for a genuine Scotty-for-Dennis send. The
 annotation is declared anyway, and correctly: the seam is the right one and
 the field is where the value belongs the moment the delegated-publish path
 exists. Closing it needs an s2s publish that carries the caller's exchanged
 token, which the generated publisher does not offer today. Written up in
 workers/big8-p1-messaging-questions.md rather than hand-rolled around.

fields.name: request_id
fields.description:
request_id is the JOIN KEY to the accounting plane — the same value
 accountingrecord.AccountingRecord carries under the same name with the same
 EQ query_field, so "which accounting rows belong to the request that sent
 this message" is one predicate asked of two record types.

 Empty is legitimate: a call with no authenticated Caller has none to read.

fields.name: agent_received
fields.description:
agent_received is the delivery ACK, written by the consuming agent after it
 processes this delivery. Unset at publish — this service never writes it.

message.name: AgentReceivedReceipt
message.description:
AgentReceivedReceipt is the delivery ACK — the agent (scotty, the mailbox
 service) took the record off the topic and processed it. Written by the
 consumer, never by the sender or by this service.

 It is the ACK, not a copy of it: there is one event here, not a delivery ACK
 plus a receipt derived from it.

fields.name: received_at_ms
fields.description:
received_at_ms is when the consuming agent completed processing — the same
 instant it commits its consumer-group offset, since committing before
 processing is exactly the discipline the queue semantics forbid.

fields.name: received_by
fields.description: received_by is the SPIFFE identity of the consuming agent instance.

fields.name: human_viewed
fields.description:
human_viewed is the separately-typed human signal. Unset at publish, and
 unset for as long as the person has not looked, which is the normal state
 of a delivered message.

message.name: HumanViewedReceipt
message.description:
HumanViewedReceipt fires when the actual person looked at the message. A
 distinct signal from AgentReceivedReceipt above: an agent can have ACKed a
 message hours before a human sees it, and business-hours-deferred
 presentation makes that gap the normal case rather than the exception.

 Presentation is a passive pull label — the reader is told "viewed", never
 pushed a notification. That is the design already built for tickets
 (decisions/ticket-read-receipts-2026-08-30.md), relocated to where it
 belongs.

fields.name: viewed_at_ms
fields.description: viewed_at_ms is when the person actually looked.

fields.name: viewed_by
fields.description:
viewed_by is the principal subject of the person who looked. It is normally
 equal to Message.recipient — a delivery is viewed by its addressee — but it
 is stored rather than assumed, because a delegate viewing on someone's
 behalf is a real case and an inferred value could not tell the two apart.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT, by EXACT string equality against the
 caller's namespace claim (never the level-or-below containment the
 administrative namespace rule uses). It is the tenant half of the identity
 `recipient` carries the subject half of: that field's (spec.store_principal)
 answers "are these MY rows", this one answers "is this MY tenant".

 MANDATORY, not opt-in: tacplus (ValidateRecordNamespaceAnnotations) fails
 generation for any (spec.record) declaring no such field, on the reasoning
 that the record nobody remembered to annotate is exactly the one that leaks.

 TWO DIFFERENT ENFORCEMENTS, and they are not the same failure:
   - WRITE (this record's publish path). eventbus's PublishHandler stamps
     this field from the publishing token's namespace claim and REFUSES the
     publish with PERMISSION_DENIED when the token carries none. Stamp-or-
     refuse, deliberately not stamp-if-empty: a row published with an empty
     namespace is a row no legitimate caller can ever read.
   - READ (stratum's record query plane, c2s half). The generated egress
     filter holds every row to the reader's own claim, and a row that fails
     the comparison HALTS THE JVM rather than failing the one call — the
     filter is the backstop behind the store's own query, so it firing means
     that query is broken.

 Bounded like every other string here. Not a (spec.query_field): the field
 exists to be the egress boundary, and making it a caller-supplied predicate
 is not what a boundary is.

 submission N separately-keyed records rather than N copies of one.

 reconstruct to ACK a delivery is exactly (which message, for whom), so
 deriving it means an agent that knows both never has to have been told the
 id. It is also what makes the fan-out replay-safe — a retried submission
 regenerates the same delivery ids rather than a second set of rows.

fields.name: message_id
fields.description:
message_id groups the N deliveries of ONE submission. EQ-filterable,

fields.name: sender
fields.description:
sender is who sent it — the authenticated principal subject bound by the
 (spec.principal) field on SendMessageRequest below, never a caller-written
 string.

fields.name: recipient
fields.description:
recipient is THE recipient this delivery is for — one of `recipients`
 below, and the half of delivery_id that varies across the fan-out.

 half. spiffe_id below is the record's declared owner but is the PUBLISHER —
 eventbus stamps messaging's own service identity onto it — so filtering a
 user's reads on that field would show every user nothing. `sender` is the
 other candidate and is the wrong one: a mailbox read is "messages addressed
 to me", so the field the generated egress filter holds a caller's reads to
 must be the addressee.

 sent messages through this record's c2s plane, because only one field may
 carry (spec.store_principal) and this is it. Sent-items is a mailbox

 second read path for it here would be inventing that service's shape.

fields.name: recipients
fields.description:

 SAME list on all N deliveries. `recipient` above says which one this row is
 for; this says who else got it.

fields.name: subject
fields.description: subject is the message's subject line.

fields.name: text
fields.description: text is the message body. Free text, and nothing parses it — see ticket_id.

fields.name: ticket_id
fields.description:
ticket_id OPTIONALLY references the ticket this message pertains to.

 display have to associate a message with its ticket to act, and the
 standing rule is that anything that must be parsed to be acted on should
 have been a field. Optional because most messages pertain to no ticket, and
 EQ-filterable because "every message about this ticket" is the question the
 field exists to answer.

 stays entirely inside Ticket. That is what keeps this type stable.

fields.name: sent_at_ms
fields.description:
sent_at_ms is the business clock — when the sender submitted — and the
 RANGE criterion, because "my messages from last week" is the question a
 mailbox asks.

 Identical across all N deliveries of one submission: they were one act.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner. The name is LOAD-BEARING: eventbus's topic
 discovery matches the literal field name "spiffe_id" of string type when it
 decides which topics get publisher-identity stamping, so renaming this
 field silently turns the stamping off.

 It holds MESSAGING'S OWN service identity, not the sender's, because the
 publish is s2s from this service — that is the direct consequence of the
 SUPERSEDED ruling. `sender` above is where the human is.

fields.name: spiffe_actor
fields.description:
spiffe_actor is the ORIGIN signal: the delegate that made the call, stamped
 by EventBus from the publishing token's `act` claim at publish time.

   "a message is marked as originating from the user directly or from the
    user's Scotty acting on their behalf... A message sent by
    Scotty-for-Dennis carries `act` populated; one Dennis sends directly
    doesn't." — decisions/messaging-vs-ticketing-2026-08-31.md

 The service does not set it and must not: like spiffe_id above, a value
 written here would be a claim about identity that nothing verified.
 Provenance only — sys/spec.proto forbids wiring it into a principal.

 model, where the user published to EventBus DIRECTLY and EventBus saw the
 user's own delegated token. Under the corrected model the publish is s2s
 from messaging, so the token EventBus stamps from is messaging's own
 service token and carries no `act` claim at all — this field will be empty
 in the ordinary case, including for a genuine Scotty-for-Dennis send. The
 annotation is declared anyway, and correctly: the seam is the right one and
 the field is where the value belongs the moment the delegated-publish path
 exists. Closing it needs an s2s publish that carries the caller's exchanged
 token, which the generated publisher does not offer today. Written up in
 workers/big8-p1-messaging-questions.md rather than hand-rolled around.

fields.name: request_id
fields.description:
request_id is the JOIN KEY to the accounting plane — the same value
 accountingrecord.AccountingRecord carries under the same name with the same
 EQ query_field, so "which accounting rows belong to the request that sent
 this message" is one predicate asked of two record types.

fields.name: agent_received
fields.description:
agent_received is the delivery ACK, written by the consuming agent after it
 processes this delivery. Unset at publish — this service never writes it.

message.name: AgentReceivedReceipt
message.description:
AgentReceivedReceipt is the delivery ACK — the agent (scotty, the mailbox
 service) took the record off the topic and processed it. Written by the
 consumer, never by the sender or by this service.

 It is the ACK, not a copy of it: there is one event here, not a delivery ACK
 plus a receipt derived from it.

fields.name: received_at_ms
fields.description:
received_at_ms is when the consuming agent completed processing — the same
 instant it commits its consumer-group offset, since committing before
 processing is exactly the discipline the queue semantics forbid.

fields.name: received_by
fields.description: received_by is the SPIFFE identity of the consuming agent instance.

fields.name: human_viewed
fields.description:
human_viewed is the separately-typed human signal. Unset at publish, and
 unset for as long as the person has not looked, which is the normal state
 of a delivered message.

message.name: HumanViewedReceipt
message.description:
HumanViewedReceipt fires when the actual person looked at the message. A
 distinct signal from AgentReceivedReceipt above: an agent can have ACKed a
 message hours before a human sees it, and business-hours-deferred
 presentation makes that gap the normal case rather than the exception.

 pushed a notification. That is the design already built for tickets
 (decisions/ticket-read-receipts-2026-08-30.md), relocated to where it
 belongs.

fields.name: viewed_at_ms
fields.description: viewed_at_ms is when the person actually looked.

fields.name: viewed_by
fields.description:
viewed_by is the principal subject of the person who looked. It is normally
 equal to Message.recipient — a delivery is viewed by its addressee — but it
 is stored rather than assumed, because a delegate viewing on someone's
 behalf is a real case and an inferred value could not tell the two apart.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT, by EXACT string equality against the
 caller's namespace claim (never the level-or-below containment the
 administrative namespace rule uses). It is the tenant half of the identity
 `recipient` carries the subject half of: that field's (spec.store_principal)
 answers "are these MY rows", this one answers "is this MY tenant".

   - WRITE (this record's publish path). eventbus's PublishHandler stamps

     refuse, deliberately not stamp-if-empty: a row published with an empty

     the comparison HALTS THE JVM rather than failing the one call — the
     filter is the backstop behind the store's own query, so it firing means
     that query is broken.

 Bounded like every other string here. Not a (spec.query_field): the field
 exists to be the egress boundary, and making it a caller-supplied predicate
 is not what a boundary is.

types.name: MessagingConfigState
types.description:
MessagingConfigState is the state boundary for messaging service configuration.
 Auto-injected by tacplus from (spec.grpc_config) annotation.

message.name: Config
message.description: Config is delivered by kernel at startup and on every change.

fields.name: max_recipients
fields.description:
max_recipients bounds the recipient fan-out of ONE submission, and it is a
 resource limit on the service, not a business rule: N recipients means N
 publishes, so an unbounded list is an unbounded amount of work bought with
 one RPC. Held in config rather than as a constant for the same reason
 tasks.Config.max_open_tasks is — changing it in kernel must change
 behaviour with no redeploy.

 It must not exceed SendMessageRequest.recipients' assert_max_size (256):
 the two describe the same cap and the generated request validation is the
 hard edge, so a config above it could never take effect.

types.name: SendMessageRequest

fields.name: sender
fields.description:
sender is (spec.principal): the generated wrapper resolves the
 authenticated caller's subject and stamps it when the field is empty,
 accepts it when it matches, and refuses with INVALID_ARGUMENT when it
 differs. A caller therefore cannot send AS someone else, and the handler
 does not check — there is nothing left to check.

fields.name: recipients
fields.description:
recipients is who the message is for. Every entry becomes its own delivery
 and its own publish.

 Bounded at 256 here and at Config.max_recipients (default 64) at runtime;
 this is the hard edge and that is the tunable one, which is why the config
 field may not exceed this number.

fields.name: ticket_id
fields.description:
ticket_id optionally associates this message with a ticket. See
 Message.ticket_id — a field, never parsed out of `text`.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is (spec.namespace): the ingest twin of Message.namespace's
 (spec.store_namespace), and the WRITE half of the namespace paired control.
 The generated wrapper resolves the caller's verified namespace claim and
   - stamps it when this field is empty,
   - accepts it when it matches,
   - REFUSES with INVALID_ARGUMENT when it differs.
 An unauthenticated caller on a namespace-bearing RPC is UNAUTHENTICATED.

 So a caller cannot address a send into another tenant, and the refusal
 happens before the handler runs. That is the write-side behaviour; the
 read-side backstop crashes instead, and the difference is deliberate — see
 Message.namespace.

types.name: SendMessageResponse

fields.name: message_id
fields.description: message_id groups the deliveries this call produced.

fields.name: delivery_ids
fields.description:
delivery_ids is one id per recipient, in the order the recipients were
 given, and its LENGTH is the fan-out count. Returning them rather than just
 the message_id is what lets a caller (or a test) assert that N recipients
 produced N separately-keyed deliveries without reading the topic.

rpcs.description:
SendMessage submits one message and fans it out to its recipients.

 Send, not Submit: the RPC verb registry is CLOSED
 (tacplus/pkg/internal/common/verbs/registry.json) and Submit is not in it,
 with no synonym mapping. Send is the registered verb for point-to-point
 delivery, and its boundary note — "NOT Publish; one intended recipient or
 channel endpoint" — is exactly right here: the recipients are named
 parties, and the fan-out across them is the N point-to-point deliveries
 this RPC produces. Publish would name the OTHER axis, the topic one, which
 is EventBus's and not this RPC's. The decision doc's "(e.g. `Submit`)" was
 an illustration, not a name.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Publish; one intended recipient or channel endpoint.

rpcs.description:
BrokerMessagingMcpSession carries one Model Context Protocol session for Messaging over a
 single bidirectional stream: one complete JSON-RPC frame per stream message,
 request frames in and response frames out, for the life of the session.

 Generated, never declared: Messaging has at least one RPC_PRINCIPAL_MCP rpc, and this
 is the only channel those tools are reachable through. Bidirectional because an
 MCP session is stateful — it opens with an initialize handshake and holds the
 negotiated protocol version after it — so a unary call would repeat that
 handshake per tool call.
rpcs.verb_definition: Coordinate a mediated exchange between two parties.
rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Proxy; owns matching, relay, or completion semantics rather than transparently forwarding one backend call.

rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Send; fan-out to topic subscribers.

rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT Watch; use Watch only for generated collection snapshot/upsert/delete streams.

rpcs.verb_boundary: NOT List/Watch; returns one resource or not-found and must not mutate state.

types.name: AuthorizeRequest
types.description: AuthorizeRequest initiates an OAuth2 flow.

fields.name: provider_index
fields.description: provider_index selects which configured provider to use.

fields.name: callback_url
fields.description:
callback_url is where the user is sent after successful authentication.
 This is the originating microservice's URL (e.g. "https://sentinel:9000/").
constraints: must be a valid URL (scheme: URL_SCHEME_HTTPS)

fields.name: session_id
fields.description:
session_id is set when the OAuth flow was initiated by a CLI client.
 If present, the callback handler writes the minted token to OAuthState
 for delivery to the matching bidi stream.

fields.name: nonce
fields.description:
nonce is a caller-supplied OIDC nonce, relayed verbatim to the IDP's
 authorization endpoint so the IDP echoes it back as the id_token's
 `nonce` claim (forwarded to kernel as `origin_nonce`). Set by a device
 proving possession of its key — the value is then the key's RFC 7638
 thumbprint, which CreateTenantUserLink's device side compares against.
 Empty means no nonce is requested and no `nonce` param is sent at all,
 which is every login that is not proving device possession.

types.name: AuthorizeResponse
types.description: AuthorizeResponse contains the IDP redirect URL.

fields.name: redirect_url
fields.description: redirect_url is the full OAuth2 authorization URL to redirect the user to.
constraints: must be a valid URL (scheme: URL_SCHEME_HTTPS)

types.name: CallbackRequest
types.description: CallbackRequest handles the OAuth2 authorization code callback.

fields.name: code
fields.description: code is the authorization code from the IDP.

fields.name: state
fields.description: state is the anti-CSRF state parameter.

types.name: CallbackResponse
types.description: CallbackResponse contains the minted tokens and the callback destination.

fields.name: refresh_token
fields.description: refresh_token is the long-lived refresh token signed by kernel.

fields.name: access_token
fields.description: access_token is the short-lived access token for immediate use.

fields.name: callback_url
fields.description: callback_url is the original URL to redirect the user back to.
constraints: must be a valid URL (scheme: URL_SCHEME_HTTPS)

fields.name: access_token_expires_in
fields.description: access_token_expires_in is the access token lifetime in seconds.

fields.name: refresh_token_expires_in
fields.description: refresh_token_expires_in is the refresh token lifetime in seconds.

types.name: ClaimMatcher
types.description:
ClaimMatcher routes users arriving via a cluster-level shared IDP to this tenant.
 The token has already been validated against the cluster IDP before matching.

fields.name: provider_issuer_url
fields.description: provider_issuer_url identifies which cluster IDP this rule applies to.
constraints: must be a valid URL (scheme: URL_SCHEME_HTTPS)

fields.name: claim_key
fields.description: claim_key is the JWT claim name (e.g. "hd", "email").

fields.name: claim_value
fields.description: claim_value is the expected value (e.g. "mycompany.com").

types.name: ClusterOAuthConfig
types.description:
ClusterOAuthConfig holds cluster-level shared IDP configuration.
 Configured once by a cluster admin; shared across all tenants.
 Delivered to the oauth service alongside per-tenant OAuthTenantConfig slices.

message.name: ClusterOAuthProvider
message.description:
ClusterOAuthProvider describes a shared IDP (e.g. Google, GitHub) available
 to all tenants. Tenants route users from these IDPs via ClaimMatcher entries.

fields.name: issuer_url
fields.description: issuer_url is the OpenID Connect issuer (e.g. "https://accounts.google.com").
constraints: must be a valid URL (scheme: URL_SCHEME_HTTPS)

fields.name: client_id
fields.description: client_id is the shared OAuth app client identifier.

fields.name: client_secret
fields.description: client_secret is the sensitive OAuth app secret; supplied by cluster admin.

fields.name: allowed_scopes
fields.description: allowed_scopes are the OAuth2 scopes requested from this IDP.

fields.name: jwks_uri
fields.description: jwks_uri overrides the auto-discovered JWKS endpoint.
constraints: must be a valid URL (scheme: URL_SCHEME_HTTPS)

fields.name: ca_pem
fields.description: ca_pem is an optional PEM-encoded CA certificate for self-signed IDPs.

fields.name: enable
fields.description: enable enables or disables this cluster IDP.

 authenticated and wants to authorize a CLI session.

 If empty, the system default CA bundle is used.

fields.name: allowed_redirect_uri_prefixes
fields.description:
allowed_redirect_uri_prefixes is the operator-configured allowlist of
 callback URLs this provider may redirect a user back to. AuthorizeRequest
 .callback_url is caller-supplied and unauthenticated; without this list it
 would be handed to the IDP as redirect_uri verbatim, letting anyone start a
 login that delivers the authorization code to a host they control.

 Matching rule (deliberately strict, no wildcards, no URL parsing):
   - An entry that does NOT end in "/" matches only a byte-identical
     callback_url.
   - An entry that DOES end in "/" additionally matches any callback_url
     that begins with it. The trailing slash is what makes the prefix end on
     a path boundary, so "https://legit.example.com/app/" cannot be
     satisfied by "https://legit.example.com/app-evil/..." and
     "https://legit.example.com/app" cannot be satisfied by
     "https://legit.example.comX/".

 Comparison is exact and case-sensitive. There is no implicit default: a
 provider with an empty list authorizes nothing, so the service fails closed
 if the field is ever missing at runtime.

fields.name: nonce_expire_seconds
fields.description:
nonce_expire_seconds is how long OAuth2 nonces/state remain valid.
 Nonces prevent replay attacks in the authorization code flow.
 Minimum: 1 second. Maximum: 86400 (24 hours). Default: 300 (5 minutes).

fields.name: jwk_refetch_interval_seconds
fields.description:
jwk_refetch_interval_seconds is the minimum interval between JWKS fetches
 from the same external IDP. Prevents excessive outbound requests.
 Default: 300 (5 minutes).

fields.name: session_timeout_seconds
fields.description:
session_timeout_seconds is how long an unauthenticated bidi session
 waits for token delivery before timing out.
 Minimum: 30 seconds. Maximum: 600 (10 minutes). Default: 300 (5 minutes).

fields.name: refresh_token_lifetime_seconds
fields.description:
refresh_token_lifetime_seconds is the lifetime for long-lived refresh
 tokens issued to CLI clients. Longer than browser sessions because
 laptops may be offline for extended periods.
 Minimum: 3600 (1 hour). Maximum: 2592000 (30 days). Default: 604800 (7 days).

fields.name: auto_refresh_before_seconds
fields.description:
auto_refresh_before_seconds is how far before token expiry the service
 proactively refreshes tokens for connected daemon clients.
 Minimum: 60 (1 minute). Maximum: 86400 (1 day). Default: 3600 (1 hour).

fields.name: enable
fields.description: enable enables or disables OAuth2 authentication.

fields.name: scopes
fields.description:
scopes are the default OAuth2 scopes requested from all providers.
 If empty, defaults to ["openid", "profile", "email"].

fields.name: providers
fields.description: providers is the list of OAuth2 identity provider configurations.

fields.name: allowed_redirect_uri_prefixes
fields.description:
allowed_redirect_uri_prefixes is the operator-configured allowlist of
 callback URLs this provider may redirect a user back to. AuthorizeRequest
 .callback_url is caller-supplied and unauthenticated; without this list it
 would be handed to the IDP as redirect_uri verbatim, letting anyone start a
 login that delivers the authorization code to a host they control.

   - An entry that does NOT end in "/" matches only a byte-identical
     callback_url.
   - An entry that DOES end in "/" additionally matches any callback_url
     that begins with it. The trailing slash is what makes the prefix end on
     a path boundary, so "https://legit.example.com/app/" cannot be
     satisfied by "https://legit.example.com/app-evil/..." and
     "https://legit.example.com/app" cannot be satisfied by
     "https://legit.example.comX/".

fields.name: nonce_expire_seconds
fields.description:
nonce_expire_seconds is how long OAuth2 nonces/state remain valid.
 Nonces prevent replay attacks in the authorization code flow.
 Minimum: 1 second. Maximum: 86400 (24 hours). Default: 300 (5 minutes).

fields.name: jwk_refetch_interval_seconds
fields.description:
jwk_refetch_interval_seconds is the minimum interval between JWKS fetches
 from the same external IDP. Prevents excessive outbound requests.
 Default: 300 (5 minutes).

types.name: SessionRequest
types.description: SessionRequest is sent by the client on the bidi stream.

fields.description:
session_id initiates the session (first message on the stream).
 Must be a cryptographically random identifier (min 32 bytes, hex-encoded).

 local daemon; access and service tokens remain derived, short-lived, and
 memory-only.
