types.name: Config
types.description:
Config is the single configuration type for all services.

 Bootstrap fields (endpoints, instance_id, private_key, trusted_cas) are loaded
 from YAML at boot and used to connect to the cluster.

 Runtime fields (ping_interval_ms, rebalance_interval_ms, listen_address,
 max_request_size, request_timeout_seconds, logger, shutdown_timeout_seconds)
 are delivered by the cluster via ServiceConfigState and can change at any time.

 TLS certificates are obtained automatically by the servicemanager via X509Mint
 after token exchange — they are not part of the config.

fields.name: endpoints
fields.description:
Cluster endpoints. Set in bootstrap file; can be updated at runtime
 via ServiceConfigState to add/remove endpoints dynamically.

message.name: Host
message.description:
Host identifies a network endpoint by hostname/IP and port.
 The host field accepts either an FQDN or an IP address (v4/v6).

fields.name: host
fields.description: Hostname or IP address (e.g. "api.example.com" or "10.0.0.1").
constraints: must be a valid hostname or IP address

fields.name: port
fields.description: Port number (1-65535).
constraints: must be a valid network port (1-65535)

fields.name: protocol
fields.description: Transport protocol. Default TCP (zero value).

fields.name: instance_id
fields.description:
instance_id uniquely identifies this running instance/replica.
 Used for leader elections on boundaries with (spec.leader) = true.
 If empty, a random ID is generated at client creation time.

fields.name: private_key
fields.description:
private_key is used to mint throwaway bootstrap JWTs for the
 token exchange flow. The kid is in private_key.id;
 identity (subject/audience) comes from the delegate looked up
 by TokenExchanger using the matching kid.
 If absent, cloud-native authentication is attempted.

message.name: Key
message.description: Key represents a private cryptographic key (alias for ProtoKey).

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is a unique identifier for the key (corresponds to kid in JWK)

fields.name: base64
fields.description: Base64 contains the base64url-encoded PEM private key block

fields.name: created
fields.description:
Created is the Unix epoch timestamp (seconds) when the key was created
 Valid range: 1735689600 (2025-01-01) to 8045740800 (2225-01-01)

fields.name: ping_interval_ms
fields.description:
ping_interval_ms controls how often each endpoint is pinged for latency measurement.
 Default: 5000 (5 seconds)

fields.name: rebalance_interval_ms
fields.description:
rebalance_interval_ms controls how often the active connection is re-evaluated
 based on latency. Default: 10000 (10 seconds)

fields.name: listen_address
fields.description: listen_address is the bind address for the gRPC server. Default port 8443.

fields.name: max_request_size
fields.description:
max_request_size is the maximum request size in bytes.
 Must be greater than 0. Default: 10MB (10485760 bytes)

fields.name: request_timeout_seconds
fields.description:
request_timeout_seconds is the timeout for client requests.
 Must be positive. Default: 30 seconds.

fields.name: logger
fields.description:
logger configures the logger for the service.
 Controls log format (JSON/console), level, output paths, and more.

message.name: LoggerConfig
message.description:
LoggerConfig represents the configuration for a logger instance.
 It controls the output format, verbosity level, and formatting options.

 Example usage:
   - Development mode with console output and pretty printing for local debugging
   - Production mode with JSON output and no pretty printing for log aggregation

fields.name: name
fields.description: Name is the logger name/component identifier

fields.name: format
fields.description:
Format determines the output format for log messages (JSON or console)
 Default: FORMAT_JSON in production, FORMAT_CONSOLE in development

enum_values.name: FORMAT_JSON
enum_values.description: FORMAT_JSON outputs logs as JSON objects, ideal for structured logging and log aggregation systems

enum_values.name: FORMAT_CONSOLE
enum_values.description: FORMAT_CONSOLE outputs logs in a human-readable console format, ideal for development and debugging

fields.name: level
fields.description:
Level sets the minimum severity level for log messages to be output
 Messages below this level will be filtered out
 Default: LEVEL_INFO in production, LEVEL_DEBUG in development

enum_values.name: LEVEL_TRACE
enum_values.description: LEVEL_TRACE is the most verbose log level, used for detailed debugging information

enum_values.name: LEVEL_DEBUG
enum_values.description: LEVEL_DEBUG is used for debugging information, less verbose than trace

enum_values.name: LEVEL_INFO
enum_values.description: LEVEL_INFO is used for informational messages about normal operations

enum_values.name: LEVEL_WARN
enum_values.description: LEVEL_WARN is used for warning messages about potentially problematic situations

enum_values.name: LEVEL_ERROR
enum_values.description: LEVEL_ERROR is used for error messages about failures and problems

fields.name: development
fields.description:
Development enables development mode which:
   - Uses console format by default
   - Enables stack traces for warnings and errors
   - Uses more human-readable timestamps
 Default: false (production mode)

fields.name: pretty_print
fields.description:
PrettyPrint enables pretty-printed output for JSON format
 This makes JSON logs more readable but increases output size
 Should be disabled in production for performance
 Default: false

fields.name: output_paths
fields.description:
OutputPaths is a list of file paths or URLs to write logs to
 Use "stdout" or "stderr" for console output
 Example: ["stdout", "/var/log/app.log"]
constraints: must be a valid file path (type: PATH_ANY)

fields.name: error_output_paths
fields.description:
ErrorOutputPaths is a list of file paths or URLs to write error logs to
 Use "stderr" for console error output
 Example: ["stderr", "/var/log/app-errors.log"]
constraints: must be a valid file path (type: PATH_ANY)

fields.name: disable_caller
fields.description:
DisableCaller disables automatic inclusion of caller information (file:line) in log entries
 Default: false (caller information is included)

fields.name: disable_stacktrace
fields.description:
DisableStacktrace disables automatic stacktraces for error-level and above log entries
 Default: false (stacktraces are included for errors)

fields.name: initial_fields
shutdown_timeout_seconds
fields.description:
shutdown_timeout_seconds is the maximum time (in seconds) to wait for graceful
 shutdown after SIGTERM before forcing immediate shutdown.
 Must be positive. Default: 30 seconds.

fields.name: max_concurrent_streams
fields.description:
max_concurrent_streams limits the number of concurrent gRPC streams per connection.
 Prevents resource exhaustion from clients opening unlimited streams.
 Default: 100. Set to 0 to use the gRPC library default (unlimited).

fields.name: max_send_msg_size
fields.description:
max_send_msg_size is the maximum response message size in bytes.
 Prevents the server from sending responses that could OOM clients.
 Default: 16MB (16777216 bytes). Set to 0 to use the gRPC library default.

fields.name: keepalive_min_time_seconds
fields.description:
keepalive_min_time_seconds is the minimum interval clients must wait between
 keepalive pings. Clients pinging more frequently are disconnected.
 Default: 30 seconds. Set to 0 to disable enforcement.

fields.name: trusted_cas
fields.description:
trusted_cas is the explicit list of CA certificates trusted for SPIFFE TLS
 verification when connecting to cluster endpoints. It must not be empty.

message.name: X509Cert
message.description:
ProtoCert represents an X.509 certificate.
 The certificate is stored as a base64-encoded PEM block.
 Use NewProtoCert() in Go with DER-encoded certificate bytes to create.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is a unique identifier for the certificate

fields.name: base64
fields.description: Base64 contains the base64url-encoded PEM certificate block

fields.name: spiffe_trust_domain
fields.description:
spiffe_trust_domain is the SPIFFE URI authority: a globally unique instance
 name for this autonomous-system instance (need not be a DNS domain).
 It must not contain '/', a scheme, query, or fragment, and carries no path.
 Service identity is built by the generated sys/spiffe helper as:
   spiffe://<spiffe_trust_domain>/system/<location_path...>/services/<service_label>
 If empty, SPIFFE IDs are not set on health reports or X509 URI SANs.

fields.name: location_path
fields.description:
location_path is this service instance's topology path under /system —
 opaque, tag-delimited, slash-separated segments, arity not fixed
 (e.g. "aws/123456789012/us-east-1a/cluster-7/team-a"). Segments follow the
 SPIFFE segment grammar and must not be reserved tags. Supplied by the
 operator/deployment from runtime config (where the service runs); it is
 not a token claim. May be empty (no topology tiers).

fields.name: disk_persistence
fields.description:
disk_persistence is an init-time/bootstrap setting that enables
 ServiceManager-owned redo-log lifecycle for generated service_store stores.

message.name: Config

 Bootstrap fields (endpoints, instance_id, private_key, trusted_cas) are loaded
 from YAML at boot and used to connect to the cluster.

 Runtime fields (ping_interval_ms, rebalance_interval_ms, listen_address,
 max_request_size, request_timeout_seconds, logger, shutdown_timeout_seconds)

enum_values.name: FORMAT_CONSOLE

RawProxyRequest forwards an arbitrary HTTP request to a remote REST API.
 Used as the generic fallback RPC for endpoints that do not yet have typed
 RPCs. The service implementation should log when this is used, signaling
 a typed RPC coverage gap.

fields.name: metadata
fields.description:
metadata is an opaque string passed to OPA for policy evaluation.
 OPA resolves the real destination URL; if empty, the service falls back to its DEFAULT_API_ENDPOINT.

fields.name: method
fields.description: method is the HTTP method to use.

fields.name: path
fields.description: path is the API path (e.g. "/repos/owner/repo/issues").

fields.name: query_params
fields.description: query_params are URL query parameters appended to the path.

fields.name: headers
fields.description:
headers are additional HTTP headers to include in the request.
 Authentication headers are injected by the service from config.

message.name: HttpHeader

fields.name: body
fields.description: body is the request body (typically JSON).

types.name: RawProxyResponse

fields.name: status_code
fields.description: status_code is the HTTP status code from the upstream API.

fields.name: headers
fields.description: headers are the response headers from the upstream API.

message.name: HttpHeader
message.description: HttpHeader is a single HTTP header name-value pair.

fields.name: body
fields.description: body is the response body (typically JSON).

types.name: HttpClientConfig
types.description:
HttpClientConfig represents configuration for an HTTP client.
 It provides settings for TLS verification, keep-alive behavior, certificates, and timeouts.
 This configuration is typically used to create HTTP clients for making outbound requests
 with specific security and performance requirements.

fields.name: disable_keep_alives
fields.description:
DisableKeepAlives, if true, disables HTTP keep-alives and will close the connection
 after each request. This can reduce server load but increases latency for repeated requests.
 Default is false (keep-alives enabled).

fields.name: root_certs
fields.description:
RootCerts is a list of X.509 certificates to use as root CAs for verifying server certificates.
 If empty, the system's default root CAs will be used.
 Use this to trust custom or internal certificate authorities.

message.name: X509Cert
message.description:
ProtoCert represents an X.509 certificate.
 The certificate is stored as a base64-encoded PEM block.
 Use NewProtoCert() in Go with DER-encoded certificate bytes to create.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is a unique identifier for the certificate

fields.name: base64
fields.description: Base64 contains the base64url-encoded PEM certificate block

fields.name: client_cert
fields.description:
ClientCert is an X.509 certificate chain with private key for client authentication.
 Use this when the server requires mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication.
 chain[0] is the leaf cert, key must be set for mTLS.

message.name: X509CertChain
message.description:
X509CertChain contains a certificate chain and optional private key.
 chain[0] is the leaf (end-entity) cert, followed by intermediates, ordered toward root.
 When key is present, the chain is a full credential suitable for TLS.

fields.name: chain
fields.description: chain[0] is the leaf (end-entity) cert, followed by intermediates, ordered toward root.

fields.name: key
fields.description: optional private key for the leaf cert; present when chain is a full credential.

message.name: Key
message.description: Key represents a private cryptographic key (alias for ProtoKey).

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is a unique identifier for the key (corresponds to kid in JWK)

fields.name: base64
fields.description: Base64 contains the base64url-encoded PEM private key block

fields.name: created
fields.description:
Created is the Unix epoch timestamp (seconds) when the key was created
 Valid range: 1735689600 (2025-01-01) to 8045740800 (2225-01-01)

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is an optional stable key for chain collections.

fields.name: timeout_seconds
fields.description:
TimeoutSeconds is the maximum time in seconds for the entire HTTP request/response cycle.
 This includes connection time, request writing, server processing, and response reading.
 A value of 0 uses the generated client default of 30 seconds.

fields.name: max_idle_conns
fields.description:
MaxIdleConns controls the maximum number of idle (keep-alive) connections across all hosts.
 A value of 0 means no limit. Default is typically 100 if not specified.

fields.name: max_idle_conns_per_host
fields.description:
MaxIdleConnsPerHost controls the maximum number of idle (keep-alive) connections per host.
 A value of 0 means use the default (typically 2). Increase for high-throughput scenarios.

fields.name: idle_conn_timeout_seconds
fields.description:
IdleConnTimeoutSeconds is the maximum time in seconds an idle connection will remain
 in the connection pool before being closed. A value of 0 means no limit.

fields.name: tls_handshake_timeout_seconds
fields.description:
TlsHandshakeTimeoutSeconds is the maximum time in seconds to wait for a TLS handshake.
 A value of 0 means no timeout. Recommended: 10 seconds.

fields.name: expect_continue_timeout_seconds
fields.description:
ExpectContinueTimeoutSeconds is the maximum time in seconds to wait for a server's
 first response headers after fully writing the request headers if the request has
 "Expect: 100-continue" header. A value of 0 means no timeout.

fields.name: response_header_timeout_seconds
fields.description:
ResponseHeaderTimeoutSeconds is the maximum time in seconds to wait for a server's
 response headers after fully writing the request (including body, if any).
 A value of 0 means no timeout.

fields.name: retry_config
fields.description:
RetryConfig configures retry behavior for HTTP requests.
 If not specified, default retry configuration will be used (3 retries, jittered exponential backoff).

message.name: RetryConfig
message.description:
RetryConfig configures retry behavior for HTTP requests with jittered exponential backoff.
 This configuration controls how failed requests are retried, including which errors
 and status codes trigger retries, and the backoff timing between attempts.

fields.name: max_retries
fields.description:
MaxRetries is the maximum number of retry attempts after the initial request.
 A value of 0 means no retries (only the initial request is made).
 Default: 3

fields.name: initial_backoff_ms
fields.description:
InitialBackoffMs is the initial backoff duration in milliseconds before the first retry.
 This value is multiplied by BackoffMultiplier for each subsequent retry.
 Default: 100ms

fields.name: max_backoff_ms
fields.description:
MaxBackoffMs is the maximum backoff duration in milliseconds.
 The backoff will never exceed this value, even after many retries.
 Default: 5000ms (5 seconds)

fields.name: backoff_multiplier
fields.description:
BackoffMultiplier is the multiplier applied to the backoff duration after each retry.
 For exponential backoff, use values like 2.0 (doubles each time).
 For linear backoff, use 1.0 (stays constant).
 Default: 2.0

fields.name: retryable_status_codes
fields.description:
RetryableStatusCodes are HTTP status codes that should trigger a retry.
 Common retryable codes: 429 (Too Many Requests), 500, 502, 503, 504.
 If empty, defaults to [429, 500, 502, 503, 504].
 Network errors (connection failures, timeouts) are always retried regardless of this setting.

types.description:
RetryConfig configures retry behavior for HTTP requests with jittered exponential backoff.
 This configuration controls how failed requests are retried, including which errors
 and status codes trigger retries, and the backoff timing between attempts.

fields.name: max_retries
fields.description:
MaxRetries is the maximum number of retry attempts after the initial request.
 A value of 0 means no retries (only the initial request is made).
 Default: 3

fields.name: initial_backoff_ms
fields.description:
InitialBackoffMs is the initial backoff duration in milliseconds before the first retry.
 This value is multiplied by BackoffMultiplier for each subsequent retry.
 Default: 100ms

fields.name: max_backoff_ms
fields.description:
MaxBackoffMs is the maximum backoff duration in milliseconds.
 The backoff will never exceed this value, even after many retries.
 Default: 5000ms (5 seconds)

fields.name: backoff_multiplier
fields.description:
BackoffMultiplier is the multiplier applied to the backoff duration after each retry.
 For exponential backoff, use values like 2.0 (doubles each time).
 For linear backoff, use 1.0 (stays constant).
 Default: 2.0

fields.name: retryable_status_codes
fields.description:
RetryableStatusCodes are HTTP status codes that should trigger a retry.
 Common retryable codes: 429 (Too Many Requests), 500, 502, 503, 504.
 If empty, defaults to [429, 500, 502, 503, 504].
 Network errors (connection failures, timeouts) are always retried regardless of this setting.

types.name: Jwk
types.description:
Jwk represents a JSON Web Key as defined in RFC 7517.
 It contains the public key parameters for RSA (e, n), EC (crv, x, y), or OKP (crv, x) keys.
 JWK is used for key distribution and verification in JSON-based protocols like JWT.

fields.name: kty
fields.description: Kty is the key type parameter (RSA, EC, or OKP)

enum_values.name: KEY_TYPE_RSA
enum_values.description: KeyTypeRsa represents an RSA key type

enum_values.name: KEY_TYPE_EC
enum_values.description: KeyTypeEc represents an Elliptic Curve key type

enum_values.name: KEY_TYPE_OKP
enum_values.description: KeyTypeOkp represents an Octet Key Pair (EdDSA) key type

fields.name: alg
fields.description: Alg is the algorithm intended for use with the key (e.g., "RS384", "ES256", "EdDSA")

fields.name: kid
fields.description: Kid is the key ID used to match keys with signatures

fields.name: use
fields.description: Use indicates the intended use of the key (sig for signatures, enc for encryption)

enum_values.name: JWK_USE_TYPE_SIG
enum_values.description: JwkUseTypeSig indicates the key is used for digital signatures

enum_values.name: JWK_USE_TYPE_ENC
enum_values.description: JwkUseTypeEnc indicates the key is used for encryption

fields.name: e
fields.description: E is the RSA public exponent (base64url encoded without padding)

fields.name: n
fields.description: N is the RSA modulus (base64url encoded without padding)

fields.name: crv
fields.description: Crv is the elliptic curve name (e.g., P-256, P-384, P-521, Ed25519)

fields.name: x
fields.description: X is the x coordinate for EC keys or the public key for OKP (base64url encoded without padding)

fields.name: y
fields.description: Y is the y coordinate for EC keys (base64url encoded without padding, not used for OKP)

fields.name: exp
fields.description:
Exp is the expiration in epoch seconds. This is not part of the JWK spec as the spec does
 not specify how to handle public key expiration.
 When stored in a collection with epoch_expiration, the state store computes TTL = exp - now
 and auto-evicts the entry on expiry.

fields.name: created
fields.description:
Created is the Unix epoch timestamp (seconds) when the key was created (optional).
 If set, valid range: 1735689600 (2025-01-01) to 8045740800 (2225-01-01)

message.name: Jwk
message.description:
Jwk represents a JSON Web Key as defined in RFC 7517.
 It contains the public key parameters for RSA (e, n), EC (crv, x, y), or OKP (crv, x) keys.
 JWK is used for key distribution and verification in JSON-based protocols like JWT.

fields.name: kty
fields.description: Kty is the key type parameter (RSA, EC, or OKP)

enum_values.name: KEY_TYPE_RSA
enum_values.description: KeyTypeRsa represents an RSA key type

enum_values.name: KEY_TYPE_EC
enum_values.description: KeyTypeEc represents an Elliptic Curve key type

enum_values.name: KEY_TYPE_OKP
enum_values.description: KeyTypeOkp represents an Octet Key Pair (EdDSA) key type

fields.name: alg
fields.description: Alg is the algorithm intended for use with the key (e.g., "RS384", "ES256", "EdDSA")

fields.name: kid
fields.description: Kid is the key ID used to match keys with signatures

fields.name: use
fields.description: Use indicates the intended use of the key (sig for signatures, enc for encryption)

enum_values.name: JWK_USE_TYPE_SIG
enum_values.description: JwkUseTypeSig indicates the key is used for digital signatures

enum_values.name: JWK_USE_TYPE_ENC
enum_values.description: JwkUseTypeEnc indicates the key is used for encryption

fields.name: e
fields.description: E is the RSA public exponent (base64url encoded without padding)

fields.name: n
fields.description: N is the RSA modulus (base64url encoded without padding)

fields.name: crv
fields.description: Crv is the elliptic curve name (e.g., P-256, P-384, P-521, Ed25519)

fields.name: x
fields.description: X is the x coordinate for EC keys or the public key for OKP (base64url encoded without padding)

fields.name: y
fields.description: Y is the y coordinate for EC keys (base64url encoded without padding, not used for OKP)

fields.name: exp
fields.description:
Exp is the expiration in epoch seconds. This is not part of the JWK spec as the spec does
 not specify how to handle public key expiration.
 When stored in a collection with epoch_expiration, the state store computes TTL = exp - now
 and auto-evicts the entry on expiry.

fields.name: created
fields.description:
Created is the Unix epoch timestamp (seconds) when the key was created (optional).
 If set, valid range: 1735689600 (2025-01-01) to 8045740800 (2225-01-01)

types.name: LoggerConfig
types.description:
LoggerConfig represents the configuration for a logger instance.
 It controls the output format, verbosity level, and formatting options.

 Example usage:
   - Development mode with console output and pretty printing for local debugging
   - Production mode with JSON output and no pretty printing for log aggregation

fields.name: name
fields.description: Name is the logger name/component identifier

fields.name: format
fields.description:
Format determines the output format for log messages (JSON or console)
 Default: FORMAT_JSON in production, FORMAT_CONSOLE in development

enum_values.name: FORMAT_JSON
enum_values.description: FORMAT_JSON outputs logs as JSON objects, ideal for structured logging and log aggregation systems

enum_values.name: FORMAT_CONSOLE
enum_values.description: FORMAT_CONSOLE outputs logs in a human-readable console format, ideal for development and debugging

fields.name: level
fields.description:
Level sets the minimum severity level for log messages to be output
 Messages below this level will be filtered out
 Default: LEVEL_INFO in production, LEVEL_DEBUG in development

enum_values.name: LEVEL_TRACE
enum_values.description: LEVEL_TRACE is the most verbose log level, used for detailed debugging information

enum_values.name: LEVEL_DEBUG
enum_values.description: LEVEL_DEBUG is used for debugging information, less verbose than trace

enum_values.name: LEVEL_INFO
enum_values.description: LEVEL_INFO is used for informational messages about normal operations

enum_values.name: LEVEL_WARN
enum_values.description: LEVEL_WARN is used for warning messages about potentially problematic situations

enum_values.name: LEVEL_ERROR
enum_values.description: LEVEL_ERROR is used for error messages about failures and problems

fields.name: development
fields.description:
Development enables development mode which:
   - Uses console format by default
   - Enables stack traces for warnings and errors
   - Uses more human-readable timestamps
 Default: false (production mode)

fields.name: pretty_print
fields.description:
PrettyPrint enables pretty-printed output for JSON format
 This makes JSON logs more readable but increases output size
 Should be disabled in production for performance
 Default: false

fields.name: output_paths
fields.description:
OutputPaths is a list of file paths or URLs to write logs to
 Use "stdout" or "stderr" for console output
 Example: ["stdout", "/var/log/app.log"]
constraints: must be a valid file path (type: PATH_ANY)

fields.name: error_output_paths
fields.description:
ErrorOutputPaths is a list of file paths or URLs to write error logs to
 Use "stderr" for console error output
 Example: ["stderr", "/var/log/app-errors.log"]
constraints: must be a valid file path (type: PATH_ANY)

fields.name: disable_caller
fields.description:
DisableCaller disables automatic inclusion of caller information (file:line) in log entries

types.name: McpRequest
types.description: McpRequest carries one JSON-RPC frame from an MCP client to the service.

fields.name: payload
fields.description:
payload is one complete JSON-RPC 2.0 message, serialized.

 Client frames are tool calls and protocol handshakes, both small; the
 bound is a ceiling on a malformed or hostile frame, not a working limit.

types.name: McpResponse
types.description: McpResponse carries one JSON-RPC frame from the service back to the client.

fields.name: payload
fields.description:
payload is one complete JSON-RPC 2.0 message, serialized.

 the 4 MiB gRPC message default so that a frame the service is willing to

 over-size result into a JSON-RPC error on that request rather than failing

message.name: Jwk
message.description:
Jwk represents a JSON Web Key as defined in RFC 7517.
 It contains the public key parameters for RSA (e, n), EC (crv, x, y), or OKP (crv, x) keys.
 JWK is used for key distribution and verification in JSON-based protocols like JWT.

fields.name: kty
fields.description: Kty is the key type parameter (RSA, EC, or OKP)

enum_values.name: KEY_TYPE_RSA
enum_values.description: KeyTypeRsa represents an RSA key type

enum_values.name: KEY_TYPE_EC
enum_values.description: KeyTypeEc represents an Elliptic Curve key type

enum_values.name: KEY_TYPE_OKP
enum_values.description: KeyTypeOkp represents an Octet Key Pair (EdDSA) key type

fields.name: alg
fields.description: Alg is the algorithm intended for use with the key (e.g., "RS384", "ES256", "EdDSA")

fields.name: kid
fields.description: Kid is the key ID used to match keys with signatures

fields.name: use
fields.description: Use indicates the intended use of the key (sig for signatures, enc for encryption)

enum_values.name: JWK_USE_TYPE_SIG
enum_values.description: JwkUseTypeSig indicates the key is used for digital signatures

enum_values.name: JWK_USE_TYPE_ENC
enum_values.description: JwkUseTypeEnc indicates the key is used for encryption

fields.name: e
fields.description: E is the RSA public exponent (base64url encoded without padding)

fields.name: n
fields.description: N is the RSA modulus (base64url encoded without padding)

fields.name: crv
fields.description: Crv is the elliptic curve name (e.g., P-256, P-384, P-521, Ed25519)

fields.name: x
fields.description: X is the x coordinate for EC keys or the public key for OKP (base64url encoded without padding)

fields.name: y
fields.description: Y is the y coordinate for EC keys (base64url encoded without padding, not used for OKP)

fields.name: exp
fields.description:
Exp is the expiration in epoch seconds. This is not part of the JWK spec as the spec does
 not specify how to handle public key expiration.
 When stored in a collection with epoch_expiration, the state store computes TTL = exp - now
 and auto-evicts the entry on expiry.

fields.name: created
fields.description:
Created is the Unix epoch timestamp (seconds) when the key was created (optional).
 If set, valid range: 1735689600 (2025-01-01) to 8045740800 (2225-01-01)

types.name: AccountingRecordFilter
AccountingRecordWatchChange

message.name: AccountingRecord
message.description:
AccountingRecord is one completed RPC, stored in full by stratum.

 Every service in the fleet is a producer, so the s2s surface is open to all
 service identities. There is no c2s surface: accounting rows are written by
 the chassis, never by a browser client.

fields.name: accounting_id
fields.description: accounting_id is the record key: one row per accounting event.

fields.name: request_id
fields.description:
request_id is THE correlation key — the x-request-id the gateway generates
 and every hop forwards. The EQ query_field is what lets a caller ask "which
 accounting rows belong to the request that wrote this row", which is the
 whole reason this record exists rather than a log line.

fields.name: source_id
fields.description:
source_id identifies the emitting process ("{service_id}-{instance_id}"),
 copied verbatim from accounting.Event.source_id.

fields.name: timestamp_ms
fields.description: timestamp_ms is the RANGE criterion — "everything in this window".

fields.name: level
fields.description:
level is carried on the envelope so a consumer can filter without
 inspecting the payload; same reasoning applies to the stored row.

fields.name: method
fields.description: method is the RPC that was accounted for.

fields.name: code
fields.description: code is the gRPC status code the call completed with.

fields.name: duration_ms
fields.description: duration_ms is the measured call duration.

fields.name: principal_sub
fields.description:
principal_sub is the verified human principal behind the call — the claim
 the Authorizer actually checked, not a caller-written header. Caller-decided
 redaction, the same leg TaskActivity.created_by exercises: redacted by
 default, raw only for a caller holding a matching data grant.
 It is also the ROW'S OWNING PRINCIPAL for the record query plane's c2s half:
 (spec.store_principal) is what the generated wrapper filters a user's reads
 down to, and it must name the HUMAN, not spiffe_id below. spiffe_id is the
 emitting service, so filtering on it would narrow every user to the rows it
 emitted itself — which for a human is none. The two annotations disagree on
 purpose and this one wins, exactly as sys/spec.proto describes.

 The row filter runs BEFORE the redaction above, on the raw stored value, so
 a caller without the data grant is still matched against its own principal
 rather than against a redacted string.
 NOT a (spec.query_field), deliberately, and that is a real tension rather
 than an oversight. Making it an EQ criterion is what would carry the row
 filter into the plane's SIZE-ONLY RPCs — Get<T>Count returns a number over
 the handle's predicate and no rows, so no egress filter can narrow it — but
 ValidateDataEntitlementAnnotations refuses a field that is both
 (spec.redact) and (spec.query_field), because a filterable field defeats
 redaction. That refusal is right for the S2S half of the plane, where no
 per-caller pin applies and a peer could filter on this field freely.

 So accounting ROWS are filtered to the caller at egress and accounting
 COUNTS are not. Closing that needs a per-surface criterion (c2s-only,
 wrapper-pinned) which does not exist today; it is written up in the item 2
 report rather than bought by weakening the redaction rule.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner: the EMITTING SERVICE's identity, not the end
 user's (the human principal is principal_sub above). The field name is
 load-bearing — eventbus's topic discovery matches the LITERAL name
 "spiffe_id" of string type to decide which topics get publisher-identity
 stamping, so renaming it silently turns the stamping off.

fields.name: store_epoch_ms
fields.description:
store_epoch_ms is this row's LAST-WRITE clock, Unix milliseconds, owned and
 stamped by the generated wrapper — a producer that supplies one is refused
 (INVALID_ARGUMENT), so the value can never be caller-influenced.

 It is what makes memory/disk tiering possible: the residency clock is
 measured from this clock, and it is the predicate the memory and disk legs
 partition the query on.

 NOT timestamp_ms: that is the emitting service's business clock. Two
 different clocks; only this one is store-owned. On an append-only record
 they are written together and never diverge afterwards — which is a property
 of THIS record, not of the epoch.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT: the namespace claim of the caller
 whose RPC this row accounts for. (spec.store_namespace) is the tenant twin
 of principal_sub's (spec.store_principal) above — the same egress seam, a
 different boundary. That one answers "are these MY rows"; this one answers
 "is this MY tenant", by EXACT string equality against the caller's claim.

 MANDATORY, not opt-in: tacplus (ValidateRecordNamespaceAnnotations) fails
 generation for any (spec.record) declaring no such field, on the reasoning
 that the record nobody remembered to annotate is exactly the one that leaks.

 The filter is generated on the READ side, which is not this record's own
 s2s publish surface above: stratum's record query plane (the (spec.trait) in
 the app proto's vservices/query.proto) exposes a c2s List/Sample/Watch over
 EVERY record in the fleet, and the namespace check is spliced into each of
 them for this type. A row reaching one of those with a namespace other than
 the caller's halts the JVM rather than failing the one call.

 Bounded like every other string field on this message. Not a
 (spec.query_field): the field exists to be the egress boundary, and making
 it a caller-supplied predicate is not what a boundary is.

fields.name: principal_sub_redacted

types.name: AgentCursorFilter
AgentCursorWatchChange

message.name: AgentCursor
message.description:
AgentCursor is one row per user: everything a cycle needs to know about what
 the previous cycle did.

 IT WAS KERNEL STATE UNTIL 2026-09-25 AND IS A STRATUM RECORD NOW. The
 departure was deliberate and written up (workers/big8-p1-scotty-agent-
 questions.md §1); the ruling in decisions/kernel-no-durability-user-data-to-
 stratum-2026-09-25.md reverses it, on the ground that kernel holds no durable
 user data. Item 3 of that ruling allows "a cursor may stay if it is
 rebuildable; the owning looper decides and says why". THIS CURSOR IS NOT
 ALLOWED TO STAY, and the field that decides it is last_fencing_token below: a
 stale-write reject that does not survive a restart is not a stale-write
 reject. decisions/scottyagent-record-shapes-2026-09-25.md D1.

 WHAT THE MOVE COSTS, said here and not only in the decision record, because
 the three reasons the row was kernel state were real and only one of them has
 gone away:

   - VISIBILITY. The design record requires a write to be "visible to the very
     next cycle even if it runs moments later on a different instance". A
     record reaches stratum through an EventBus publish and an ASYNCHRONOUS
     ingest, so it is not. The per-user kernel.FencedLock still serializes the
     read-modify-write; what it can no longer do is make the previous cycle's
     write readable. This is a real weakening and it is D3 of the decision
     record — read it before changing anything in `cycle_under_lock`.
   - THE READ PATH. GONE. `(spec.record_read)` at the top of this file plus
     the s2s_read grant below generate `sm.agent_cursor_record_reader()`; the
     shared `query` trait this comment used to describe is no longer how a
     service reads its own rows.
   - THE NAMESPACE STAMP. GONE, and the old comment was wrong about the
     mechanism rather than only out of date. eventbus's PublishHandler is
     ACCEPT-or-stamp-or-refuse: a row that arrives with (spec.store_namespace)
     ALREADY SET keeps that value, and only an unset one is stamped from the
     publisher (decisions/namespace-fix-corrected-2026-09-02.md). So this
     service writes the DELIVERY's tenant onto the row exactly as it did into
     kernel state, and the row lands in the user's namespace, not in
     `/system`. See the hazard note on `namespace` below.

 AgentCycle below is the other record and is unchanged: append-shaped, never
 read back by this service, and what the design record's user-facing "Bird's
 Eye View" reads through the generated c2s record query plane.

fields.name: user
fields.description:
user is the principal this cursor belongs to, the RECORD KEY, and the
 ROW'S OWNING PRINCIPAL.

 For a message-triggered cycle it is messaging.Message.recipient — the
 ADDRESSEE, not the sender: the loop that wakes is the recipient's agent.

 (spec.store_principal) is the same annotation AgentCycle.user carries and
 it does the same job here: the generated egress filter on ListMyAgentState
 drops any row whose `user` is not the caller's own subject, on top of the
 (spec.principal) stamp that already bound the request. Belt and braces by
 construction rather than by a hand-written check, and it is what stands in
 for `private` — see the record block above.

 NO (spec.query_field). It would be redundant with the key, which already
 produces the `user` criterion on AgentCursorFilter, and a second criterion
 is exactly what takes stratum's by-key point read away (pointRead fires
 only when the key criterion is the ONLY one set).

fields.name: cycles_completed
fields.description:
cycles_completed counts the loop cycles that have finished for this user.
 Monotonic, and the source of AgentCycle.cycle below.

fields.name: last_fencing_token
fields.description:
last_fencing_token is THE FENCE, and it is what makes the lock a fencing
 lock rather than a mutex.

 A fencing token is kernel's Raft log index of the granting Acquire:
 strictly increasing over every grant of every key, never reused. A resource
 owner stores the highest token it has seen and REJECTS a write carrying a
 lower one — that, not the lock, is what makes a paused or partitioned stale
 holder safe. This field is that stored highest-seen value, and this service
 is the resource owner doing the comparing (see service.rs `write_cursor`).

 Without it, a holder that stalled long enough for its lease to lapse could
 wake up and overwrite the cursor a newer holder had already advanced. The
 lock alone narrows that window; it does not close it.

fields.name: last_cycle_at_ms
fields.description: last_cycle_at_ms is when the last completed cycle finished.

fields.name: last_instance_id
fields.description:
last_instance_id is the instance that ran it. Recorded because consecutive
 cycles for one user legitimately run on different instances and "which pod
 was that" is otherwise unanswerable after the fact — NOT because anything
 routes on it. Nothing reads this field to make a decision.

fields.name: last_wake
fields.description: last_wake is the last event that woke a cycle for this user.

message.name: WakeEvent
message.description:
WakeEvent is ONE thing that woke the loop. A cycle carries every event it
 aggregated, not just the first, so "why did you wake" has a complete answer
 even when several arrived at once.

fields.name: reason
fields.description: reason is the trigger kind.

enum_values.name: WAKE_REASON_MESSAGE
enum_values.description:
A messaging.Message arrived on this user's EventBus queue and this
 instance's consumer group took it.

fields.name: source_id
fields.description:
source_id identifies the specific event. For WAKE_REASON_MESSAGE it is the
 messaging.Message's delivery_id — the record key of the one delivery this
 wake is for, not the message_id it shares with its siblings, because the
 delivery is what this consumer group consumed.

fields.name: observed_at_ms
fields.description: observed_at_ms is when this instance took the event off the queue.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT, by exact string equality against the
 reader's namespace claim.

 (spec.store_namespace) here generates the READ-side egress filter on every
 surface that returns this row — including the MCP dispatch, which resolves
 the caller's claim itself, holds each returned row to it, and ABORTS THE
 PROCESS on a row it would otherwise have to drop. That abort is the
 designed behaviour for a genuine tenant violation, not a bug.

 WHERE THE VALUE COMES FROM, stated because it is the weak link and hiding
 it would be worse. An event-driven cycle has NO CALLER: nothing
 authenticated this work, so there is no verified claim to stamp from. The
 only tenant signal available is the consumed messaging.Message's own
 `namespace`, and this service copies that. That value is itself stamped by
 eventbus from MESSAGING'S service token rather than from the sender's
 (workers/big8-p1-messaging-questions.md §1, a fleet-wide open gap), so it
 is the right FIELD carrying a value whose provenance is not yet what the
 design intends. Copying it is still correct: it is the only tenant fact the
 event carries, and the moment tacplus grows a delegated s2s publish the
 value becomes the sender's with no change here.

 Not a query field: the field exists to BE the egress boundary, a boundary a
 caller can predicate on is not one, and since 2026-09-25 there is a second
 reason — a criterion on it would cost this type its by-key point read. See
 the record block above and D2 of the decision record.

 WHAT THE MOVE TO A RECORD CHANGED, AND WHAT IT DID NOT. Nothing about where
 the value comes from: this service still copies the delivery's namespace
 onto the row. eventbus's PublishHandler is ACCEPT-or-stamp-or-refuse — a
 row arriving with this field already set KEEPS that value, and only an
 unset one is stamped from the publishing token
 (decisions/namespace-fix-corrected-2026-09-02.md) — so the row lands in the
 USER'S tenant and the caller's own read of it matches.

 THE HAZARD IF THAT EVER STOPS BEING TRUE, because it is a process abort and
 not a dropped row: this service's own namespace is `/system`, so a cursor
 that reached the topic with this field empty would come back stamped
 `/system`, and ListMyAgentState's generated backstop aborts on a row it
 would have to drop. A delivered messaging.Message always carries a
 non-empty namespace (eventbus refuses a publish without one), which is why
 there is no guard in service.rs against a case the platform cannot produce.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner, and the NAME IS LOAD-BEARING for the same
 reason it is on AgentCycle: eventbus's topic discovery matches the literal
 field name "spiffe_id" of string type when it decides which topics get
 publisher-identity stamping, so renaming this field silently turns the
 stamping off. It holds THIS SERVICE's identity, because the publish is s2s;
 `user` above is where the person is.

 Left empty by this service on publish. No (spec.query_field): nothing reads
 a cursor by publisher — every read of this type is by key.

 WHAT THE MOVE COSTS, said here and not only in the decision record, because
 the three reasons the row was kernel state were real and only one of them has
 gone away:

   - VISIBILITY. The design record requires a write to be "visible to the very
     next cycle even if it runs moments later on a different instance". A
     record reaches stratum through an EventBus publish and an ASYNCHRONOUS
     ingest, so it is not. The per-user kernel.FencedLock still serializes the
     read-modify-write; what it can no longer do is make the previous cycle's
     write readable. This is a real weakening and it is D3 of the decision
     record — read it before changing anything in `cycle_under_lock`.
   - THE READ PATH. GONE. `(spec.record_read)` at the top of this file plus
     the s2s_read grant below generate `sm.agent_cursor_record_reader()`; the
     shared `query` trait this comment used to describe is no longer how a
     service reads its own rows.
   - THE NAMESPACE STAMP. GONE, and the old comment was wrong about the
     mechanism rather than only out of date. eventbus's PublishHandler is
     ACCEPT-or-stamp-or-refuse: a row that arrives with (spec.store_namespace)
     ALREADY SET keeps that value, and only an unset one is stamped from the
     publisher (decisions/namespace-fix-corrected-2026-09-02.md). So this
     service writes the DELIVERY's tenant onto the row exactly as it did into
     kernel state, and the row lands in the user's namespace, not in
     `/system`. See the hazard note on `namespace` below.

 AgentCycle below is the other record and is unchanged: append-shaped, never
 read back by this service, and what the design record's user-facing "Bird's
 Eye View" reads through the generated c2s record query plane.

fields.name: user
fields.description:
user is the principal this cursor belongs to, the RECORD KEY, and the
 ROW'S OWNING PRINCIPAL.

 For a message-triggered cycle it is messaging.Message.recipient — the
 ADDRESSEE, not the sender: the loop that wakes is the recipient's agent.

 (spec.store_principal) is the same annotation AgentCycle.user carries and
 it does the same job here: the generated egress filter on ListMyAgentState
 drops any row whose `user` is not the caller's own subject, on top of the
 (spec.principal) stamp that already bound the request. Belt and braces by
 construction rather than by a hand-written check, and it is what stands in
 for `private` — see the record block above.

 NO (spec.query_field). It would be redundant with the key, which already
 produces the `user` criterion on AgentCursorFilter, and a second criterion
 is exactly what takes stratum's by-key point read away (pointRead fires
 only when the key criterion is the ONLY one set).

fields.name: cycles_completed
fields.description:
cycles_completed counts the loop cycles that have finished for this user.
 Monotonic, and the source of AgentCycle.cycle below.

fields.name: last_fencing_token
fields.description:
last_fencing_token is THE FENCE, and it is what makes the lock a fencing
 lock rather than a mutex.

 A fencing token is kernel's Raft log index of the granting Acquire:
 strictly increasing over every grant of every key, never reused. A resource
 owner stores the highest token it has seen and REJECTS a write carrying a
 lower one — that, not the lock, is what makes a paused or partitioned stale
 holder safe. This field is that stored highest-seen value, and this service
 is the resource owner doing the comparing (see service.rs `write_cursor`).

 Without it, a holder that stalled long enough for its lease to lapse could
 wake up and overwrite the cursor a newer holder had already advanced. The
 lock alone narrows that window; it does not close it.

fields.name: last_cycle_at_ms
fields.description: last_cycle_at_ms is when the last completed cycle finished.

fields.name: last_instance_id
fields.description:
last_instance_id is the instance that ran it. Recorded because consecutive
 cycles for one user legitimately run on different instances and "which pod
 was that" is otherwise unanswerable after the fact — NOT because anything
 routes on it. Nothing reads this field to make a decision.

fields.name: last_wake
fields.description: last_wake is the last event that woke a cycle for this user.

message.name: WakeEvent
message.description:
WakeEvent is ONE thing that woke the loop. A cycle carries every event it
 aggregated, not just the first, so "why did you wake" has a complete answer
 even when several arrived at once.

fields.name: reason
fields.description: reason is the trigger kind.

enum_values.name: WAKE_REASON_MESSAGE
enum_values.description:
A messaging.Message arrived on this user's EventBus queue and this
 instance's consumer group took it.

fields.name: source_id
fields.description:
source_id identifies the specific event. For WAKE_REASON_MESSAGE it is the
 messaging.Message's delivery_id — the record key of the one delivery this
 wake is for, not the message_id it shares with its siblings, because the
 delivery is what this consumer group consumed.

fields.name: observed_at_ms
fields.description: observed_at_ms is when this instance took the event off the queue.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT, by exact string equality against the
 reader's namespace claim.

 (spec.store_namespace) here generates the READ-side egress filter on every
 surface that returns this row — including the MCP dispatch, which resolves
 the caller's claim itself, holds each returned row to it, and ABORTS THE
 PROCESS on a row it would otherwise have to drop. That abort is the
 designed behaviour for a genuine tenant violation, not a bug.

 WHERE THE VALUE COMES FROM, stated because it is the weak link and hiding
 it would be worse. An event-driven cycle has NO CALLER: nothing
 authenticated this work, so there is no verified claim to stamp from. The
 only tenant signal available is the consumed messaging.Message's own
 `namespace`, and this service copies that. That value is itself stamped by
 eventbus from MESSAGING'S service token rather than from the sender's
 (workers/big8-p1-messaging-questions.md §1, a fleet-wide open gap), so it
 is the right FIELD carrying a value whose provenance is not yet what the
 design intends. Copying it is still correct: it is the only tenant fact the
 event carries, and the moment tacplus grows a delegated s2s publish the
 value becomes the sender's with no change here.

 Not a query field: the field exists to BE the egress boundary, a boundary a
 caller can predicate on is not one, and since 2026-09-25 there is a second
 reason — a criterion on it would cost this type its by-key point read. See
 the record block above and D2 of the decision record.

 WHAT THE MOVE TO A RECORD CHANGED, AND WHAT IT DID NOT. Nothing about where
 the value comes from: this service still copies the delivery's namespace
 onto the row. eventbus's PublishHandler is ACCEPT-or-stamp-or-refuse — a
 row arriving with this field already set KEEPS that value, and only an
 unset one is stamped from the publishing token
 (decisions/namespace-fix-corrected-2026-09-02.md) — so the row lands in the
 USER'S tenant and the caller's own read of it matches.

 THE HAZARD IF THAT EVER STOPS BEING TRUE, because it is a process abort and
 not a dropped row: this service's own namespace is `/system`, so a cursor
 that reached the topic with this field empty would come back stamped
 `/system`, and ListMyAgentState's generated backstop aborts on a row it
 would have to drop. A delivered messaging.Message always carries a
 non-empty namespace (eventbus refuses a publish without one), which is why
 there is no guard in service.rs against a case the platform cannot produce.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner, and the NAME IS LOAD-BEARING for the same
 reason it is on AgentCycle: eventbus's topic discovery matches the literal
 field name "spiffe_id" of string type when it decides which topics get
 publisher-identity stamping, so renaming this field silently turns the
 stamping off. It holds THIS SERVICE's identity, because the publish is s2s;
 `user` above is where the person is.

 Left empty by this service on publish. No (spec.query_field): nothing reads
 a cursor by publisher — every read of this type is by key.

message.name: AgentCycle
message.description:
AgentCycle is one completed loop cycle: what woke it, when, on which
 instance, under which fencing token.

 It is the durable history the design record calls the "Bird's Eye View" —
 "an ordinary generated read surface on that record — no new mechanism". This
 file therefore declares no read RPC for it: the c2s record query plane
 generated from (spec.store_principal) and the query fields below IS that
 surface, and hand-writing a second one would be the drift the typed-contract
 argument exists to prevent.

 Append-shaped by construction: the key carries the cycle number, so a cycle
 is a new row and no cycle ever rewrites another.

 spec.record implies spec.event, so tacplus synthesizes the topic wrapper
 AgentCycleBus with topic ref scottyagent.AgentCycleBus.stream. Do NOT
 hand-write that wrapper.

fields.name: cycle_id
fields.description: cycle_id is the record key: "<user>/<cycle>".

fields.name: user
fields.description:
user is whose agent ran, and the ROW'S OWNING PRINCIPAL.

 (spec.store_principal) is what holds a caller's reads of this record to
 their own rows on the c2s query plane, and it is the reason the Bird's Eye
 View needs no filtering code: "my cycles" is the only query the plane will
 answer. `spiffe_id` below is the record's declared owner but holds THIS
 SERVICE's identity (eventbus stamps the publisher), so filtering on that
 would show every user nothing.

 The EQ criterion is what carries the filter into the plane's size-only
 RPCs, which return a number over the handle's predicate and no rows for an
 egress filter to narrow.

fields.name: cycle
fields.description: cycle is this user's monotonic cycle number, the second half of cycle_id.

fields.name: fencing_token
fields.description:

 onto the row so the history itself shows the fence: cycles for one user
 must appear in strictly increasing token order, and a row that does not is
 visible evidence of a stale holder that got through.

fields.name: woke_for
fields.description:

 observed — not just the one that started it. That is the aggregation the
 design record asks for, made legible: "multiple events can land within one
 loop cycle; they are aggregated and processed together".

 Bounded at 256 to match Config.max_events_per_cycle's ceiling.

fields.name: observed_at_ms

fields.description:

fields.description:

fields.description:

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT. MANDATORY on a (spec.record):
 tacplus's ValidateRecordNamespaceAnnotations fails generation for any
 record declaring no such field, on the reasoning that the record nobody
 remembered to annotate is exactly the one that leaks.

 Left EMPTY by this service on publish, on purpose. eventbus's

message.name: AgentEvent
message.description:
AgentEvent is the top-level event published to EventBus.
 Each event represents one hook firing in one coding-agent session.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
── Identity ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 spiffe_id is the acting principal's SUBJECT SPIFFE ID
 (spiffe://<root>/tenants/<tenant_id>/users/<sub>), the durable EventDB
 owner. Stamped by EventBus from the caller's verified token at publish
 time — not populated by clients. (Replaces the former email owner.)

fields.name: event_id
fields.description:
event_id is the globally unique identifier for this event.
 Generated server-side. Not populated by clients.

enum_values.name: SENSOR_EVENT_TYPE_SESSION_START
enum_values.description: Session lifecycle.

enum_values.name: SENSOR_EVENT_TYPE_TOOL_USE
enum_values.description: Tool use (any tool: Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Agent, etc.)

enum_values.name: SENSOR_EVENT_TYPE_SUBAGENT_START
enum_values.description: Subagent lifecycle — agent spawned or finished.

enum_values.name: SENSOR_EVENT_TYPE_TASK_COMPLETED
enum_values.description: Task lifecycle.

enum_values.name: SENSOR_EVENT_TYPE_COMPACT
enum_values.description: Context management.

enum_values.name: SENSOR_EVENT_TYPE_PROMPT
enum_values.description: User prompt submitted.

enum_values.name: SENSOR_EVENT_TYPE_STOP
enum_values.description: Stop — agent finished responding.

fields.name: store_epoch_ms
fields.description:
store_epoch_ms is this row's LAST-WRITE clock, Unix milliseconds, owned and
 stamped by the generated wrapper — a producer that supplies one is refused
 (INVALID_ARGUMENT), so the value can never be caller-influenced.

 It is what makes AgentEvent REPLAYABLE in stratum's hot tier: each node's
 redo log is partial, so recovery is a union across nodes and the epoch is
 the only clock that resolves it. Without this field the type keeps its
 in-memory replication and its quorum gate but gets no redo log at all
 (stratum's HotStoreGenerator refuses one it could not safely merge).

 NOT timestamp_ms: that is the author's business clock. Two different
 clocks; only this one is store-owned.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT — the namespace claim of the principal
 whose session produced this event. It is the tenant half of the identity
 spiffe_id carries the subject half of: spiffe_id names WHO acted, this names
 WHICH TENANT the row belongs to, and the generated egress filter holds a c2s
 read to rows matching the caller's claim by EXACT equality (never the
 level-or-below containment the administrative namespace rule uses).

 MANDATORY, not opt-in: tacplus (ValidateRecordNamespaceAnnotations) fails
 generation for any (spec.record) declaring no such field, on the reasoning
 that the record nobody remembered to annotate is exactly the one that leaks.

 The filter is generated on the READ side, which is not this record's own
 s2s publish surface above: stratum's record query plane (the (spec.trait) in
 the app proto's vservices/query.proto) exposes a c2s List/Sample/Watch over
 EVERY record in the fleet, and the namespace check is spliced into each of
 them for this type. A row reaching one of those with a namespace other than
 the caller's halts the JVM rather than failing the one call.

 Deliberately NOT projected into any transformation above: adding it there
 would widen four already-explicit column lists, which is a separate call.

types.name: AgentSessionStateFilter
AgentSessionStateWatchChange

message.name: AgentSessionState
message.description:
AgentSessionState is the CURRENT state of one coding-agent session: one row
 per session, rewritten in place every time the session moves.

 It exists because the fleet had no mutable warm record and two properties of
 the warm tier are only observable on one. AgentEvent (hot) and AccountingRecord
 (warm, append-only) are both write-once by their own nature — an event and a
 completed RPC have no later state — so nothing exercised the store epoch
 REFRESHING, which is the whole reason the epoch is a last-write clock rather
 than a creation stamp.

 A session is the natural carrier for that: it is open for as long as the agent
 is working, its status and counters change while it is open, and once it has
 ended the row is a historical record that ages out of memory exactly like an
 accounting row. Both halves of the warm window apply to it, and unlike the two
 records above it moves while it is resident.

 There is no row-mutating RPC and there is not meant to be one: rows reach the
 store by EventBus publish, so an UPDATE is a republish of the same session_id.
 The generated wrapper restamps store_epoch_ms on that republish, which is what
 puts the row back inside the residency window.

fields.name: session_id
fields.description: session_id is the record key: one row per session, not one per transition.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner — the acting principal's SUBJECT SPIFFE ID,
 stamped by EventBus from the caller's verified token, exactly as on
 AgentEvent. The literal field name is load-bearing for that stamping.

fields.name: started_at_ms
fields.description:
started_at_ms is the session's business clock, fixed at the first publish and
 NOT rewritten afterwards.

 The contrast with store_epoch_ms below is the point of this record: on an
 append-only row the two clocks are written together and never diverge, so
 nothing could tell them apart. Here they diverge on every update.

fields.name: status
fields.description: status is the session's current state — the mutable field an update carries.

fields.name: tool_use_count
fields.description:
tool_use_count is how many tool invocations the session has made so far.
 Monotonic, but rewritten in place: the row holds the running total, not one
 row per increment.

fields.name: store_epoch_ms
fields.description:
store_epoch_ms is this row's LAST-WRITE clock, Unix milliseconds, owned and
 stamped by the generated wrapper — a producer that supplies one is refused
 (INVALID_ARGUMENT), so the value can never be caller-influenced.

 On this record it MOVES. Every republish of the same session_id restamps it,
 which resets the row's residency: a session that has aged out of the memory
 window and is then updated is inside the window again, because the window is
 measured from the last write and the row was just written. That is the
 property a mutable stored record without MUTABILITY_APPEND_ONLY exists to
 state, and it is why the residency clock cannot be started_at_ms.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT — the namespace claim of the principal
 whose session this row tracks, the same value AgentEvent carries for the
 events emitted inside that session. Held to EXACT equality against the
 caller's claim by the generated c2s egress filter.

 MANDATORY on every (spec.record): tacplus fails generation for one that
 declares none (ValidateRecordNamespaceAnnotations).

 Unlike status and tool_use_count, this is NOT a field an update carries: a
 session does not change tenant. It is rewritten with the same value on every
 republish of the same session_id, which is what makes the row's tenant
 stable across the restamping described for store_epoch_ms above.

types.name: AgentSessionStateWatchEvent

message.name: AgentSessionState
message.description:
AgentSessionState is the CURRENT state of one coding-agent session: one row
 per session, rewritten in place every time the session moves.

 It exists because the fleet had no mutable warm record and two properties of
 the warm tier are only observable on one. AgentEvent (hot) and AccountingRecord
 (warm, append-only) are both write-once by their own nature — an event and a
 completed RPC have no later state — so nothing exercised the store epoch
 REFRESHING, which is the whole reason the epoch is a last-write clock rather
 than a creation stamp.

 A session is the natural carrier for that: it is open for as long as the agent
 is working, its status and counters change while it is open, and once it has
 ended the row is a historical record that ages out of memory exactly like an
 accounting row. Both halves of the warm window apply to it, and unlike the two
 records above it moves while it is resident.

 There is no row-mutating RPC and there is not meant to be one: rows reach the
 store by EventBus publish, so an UPDATE is a republish of the same session_id.
 The generated wrapper restamps store_epoch_ms on that republish, which is what
 puts the row back inside the residency window.

fields.name: session_id
fields.description: session_id is the record key: one row per session, not one per transition.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record owner — the acting principal's SUBJECT SPIFFE ID,
 stamped by EventBus from the caller's verified token, exactly as on
 AgentEvent. The literal field name is load-bearing for that stamping.

fields.name: started_at_ms
fields.description:
started_at_ms is the session's business clock, fixed at the first publish and
 NOT rewritten afterwards.

 The contrast with store_epoch_ms below is the point of this record: on an
 append-only row the two clocks are written together and never diverge, so
 nothing could tell them apart. Here they diverge on every update.

fields.name: status
fields.description: status is the session's current state — the mutable field an update carries.

fields.name: tool_use_count
fields.description:
tool_use_count is how many tool invocations the session has made so far.
 Monotonic, but rewritten in place: the row holds the running total, not one
 row per increment.

fields.name: store_epoch_ms
fields.description:
store_epoch_ms is this row's LAST-WRITE clock, Unix milliseconds, owned and
 stamped by the generated wrapper — a producer that supplies one is refused
 (INVALID_ARGUMENT), so the value can never be caller-influenced.

 On this record it MOVES. Every republish of the same session_id restamps it,
 which resets the row's residency: a session that has aged out of the memory
 window and is then updated is inside the window again, because the window is
 measured from the last write and the row was just written. That is the
 property a mutable stored record without MUTABILITY_APPEND_ONLY exists to
 state, and it is why the residency clock cannot be started_at_ms.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the row's owning TENANT — the namespace claim of the principal
 whose session this row tracks, the same value AgentEvent carries for the
 events emitted inside that session. Held to EXACT equality against the
 caller's claim by the generated c2s egress filter.

 MANDATORY on every (spec.record): tacplus fails generation for one that
 declares none (ValidateRecordNamespaceAnnotations).

 Unlike status and tool_use_count, this is NOT a field an update carries: a
 session does not change tenant. It is rewritten with the same value on every
 republish of the same session_id, which is what makes the row's tenant
 stable across the restamping described for store_epoch_ms above.

types.name: AlertFilter
AlertWatchChange

message.name: Alert
message.description:
NWS issues alerts against zones, and a zone covers many places. Storing an
 Alert per place would store the same hurricane watch once per job site in
 Harris County. So the row is keyed by NWS's own alert id and carries the zones
 it names; "alerts for this place" is a read that resolves the place's zones
 first (ListAlerts takes either form). Choice E.

 Write-once like the rest: an alert NWS UPDATEs or CANCELs arrives as a NEW
 alert row whose references name the one it supersedes. Nothing is edited in
 place, which is also why there is no "active" boolean — active is a function
 of (effective, expires, superseded) AT THE MOMENT YOU ASK, not a stored flag
 some poller has to remember to clear.

fields.name: zone_ids
fields.description:
zone_ids are the NWS zones this alert names — forecast zones, county zones,
 or both. Order is NWS's.

 A NOTE ON THE REPEATED-STRING BOUND, the same one work.Job carries:
 (spec.assert_max_size) does DOUBLE DUTY on a repeated string field — tacplus
 reads it as the element byte cap AND as the element count, and there is no
 second annotation that separates them. 256 here therefore means "at most 256
 zone ids, each at most 256 bytes". A zone id is 6 bytes; 256 zones is a wide
 hurricane watch but not an unheard-of one, and this is the number to revisit
 first if a real alert is ever truncated.

fields.name: event
fields.description:
event is NWS's event name, verbatim: "Hurricane Watch", "Flash Flood
 Warning", "Heat Advisory". NOT an enum: NWS's list is long, changes, and is
 authoritative elsewhere. A rule in Reveille matches on this string, and
 matching on the bureau's own word is more honest than matching on our lossy
 re-encoding of it. Choice F.

fields.name: severity
fields.description:
ALL FOUR CARRY (spec.assert_enum_defined), AND THAT ANNOTATION REFUSES THE
 *_UNSPECIFIED ZERO VALUE. It is worth saying at the point of use because the
 consequence is a long way from the declaration: a row stored with one of
 these left at zero is written happily by the state client and then fails
 RESPONSE validation inside the generated wrapper on every read of it,
 including every WATCH frame. That is why the ingest in services/weather/
 src/nws.rs falls back to a DECLARED value for each — UNKNOWN for the first
 three, and ALERT for message_type, which is also CAP's own default for the
 field — rather than leaving an absent value at zero.

fields.name: sent_at_ms
fields.description:
sent_at_ms is a RANGE (spec.query_field), emitting sent_at_ms_from /
 sent_at_ms_to — ListAlerts's declared window and this type's ONLY store-side
 criterion beyond the key. The other four stamps are not criteria: they are
 what `active_at_ms` is COMPUTED from, and that computation needs the
 supersession set over every alert, so narrowing on one of them in the store
 would change the answer rather than speed it up.

fields.name: sender_name
fields.description: sender_name is the issuing office ("NWS Houston/Galveston TX").

fields.name: references
fields.description:
references are the alert ids this one updates, corrects or cancels. The
 superseded rows STAY. Same rule as a renewed permit in `work` and a
 corrected document in the Doc Manager: the correction is a new row that
 points at the old one. Bounded at 256 for the same double-duty reason as
 zone_ids — an alert id is up to 256 bytes, so the count cannot be lower.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace: mandatory, `/system` on every row, no criterion. See message Place,
 including the WATCH-egress hazard note on its copy of this field.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description: spiffe_id: the publisher's identity, stamped by eventbus. See message Place.

types.name: BlobFilter
BlobLinkFilter
BlobLinkStatsFilter
BlobLinkStatsWatchChange

message.name: BlobLinkStats
message.description:
BlobLinkStats is the coarse rollup of one link's resolutions (R10).

 The counters live IN MEMORY on the pod that served the request and are
 flushed here at most once a minute per token. That is the whole design: a
 `/b/` resolve must not cost a record write, and nobody needs a resolution
 count to be exact.

 `bytes_served` is honest here in a way it could not be in the v2 cloud
 design: we serve the bytes ourselves, so we count them rather than inferring
 them from a signed URL that may or may not have been followed.

 TWO PODS, TWO COUNTERS. Each pod flushes what it served, and a flush is a
 read-modify-write of this row — so the row is the SUM only as of the last
 flush either pod made. Exactness was never on offer for an in-memory counter;
 what matters is that a flush never loses another pod's contribution, which is
 why it reads before it adds.

fields.name: token_hash
fields.description:
token_hash is the key, and the same key BlobLink carries — the two rows are
 one link's two halves, split because the stats half is rewritten on a
 minute cadence and the link half is written once.

types.name: BlobLinkWatchChange

message.name: BlobLink
message.description:
BlobLink is one shareable URL, keyed by the HASH of its token (R7).

 THE RAW TOKEN APPEARS NOWHERE PERSISTENT. It is returned once, by the call
 that minted it, and this row holds only `sha256(token)`; ListLinks returns no
 tokens, and the gateway redacts `/b/*` and `/upload/*` paths from its logs.
 So a reader of the record store — or of a log, or of a backup — cannot
 resolve any link.

 REVOCATION IS IMMEDIATE, which is v3's improvement over the v2 signed-URL
 design: we serve the bytes, so `revoked_ms` is checked on every resolve
 rather than waiting for a cloud URL to expire. It is kept rather than deleted
 so an audit can still say a link existed.

fields.name: token_hash
fields.description:
token_hash is the record key: the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the raw token.
 A resolve hashes what arrived in the path and looks up THAT, so the lookup
 key is not a secret even though the path is.

fields.name: blob_id
fields.description: blob_id is the Blob this link resolves to.

fields.name: filename
fields.description:
filename is what `Content-Disposition` offers, and the ONLY source of it
 (R8) — never a client-supplied header, never a query parameter. Validated
 at mint: a basename, no CR/LF, quote, backslash, semicolon, control
 character or path separator.

enum_values.name: LINK_POLICY_BEARER
enum_values.description:
BEARER: whoever holds the token. The only policy today (R7); SAME_TENANT
 and FLEET_ONLY are additive later and need a caller identity on the `/b/`
 path, which BEARER deliberately does not have.

fields.name: expires_ms
fields.description:
expires_ms is 0 for a durable shared link and non-zero for the short-lived
 one the owner mints for its own use. Checked on resolve alongside
 revoked_ms; the two are indistinguishable to the caller, who gets a 404
 either way.

fields.name: revoked_ms
fields.description:
revoked_ms is when the owner revoked the link, 0 while live. The row is
 KEPT — see the type comment.

types.name: BlobWatchChange

message.name: Blob
message.description:
Blob is one promoted file: bytes that are fsynced and renamed into place on
 BOTH pods. A Blob row never points at bytes that are not on both pods (R9).

 IMMUTABLE AND CONTENT-ADDRESSED, PER TENANT (R5). Identity is
 `(group, namespace, content_hash)` and dedup is within a tenant and group
 only: two tenants holding the same bytes hold two files and each pays. A
 global key would have been a cross-tenant content oracle — ask whether a hash
 exists and learn that someone else has the document — and it contradicted
 DocHashIndex's own per-namespace rule.

 NO VERSIONING. A new version is a new blob and the consumer moves its own
 pointer. The filename is the consumer's and lives on BlobLink, not here.

fields.name: blob_id
fields.description:
blob_id is the record key and the file's path: `<group>/<ns>/<sha256-hex>`.
 Carried as one string rather than derived on read because it IS the key,
 and a key a reader has to assemble from three fields is a key two callers
 can assemble differently.

fields.name: group
fields.description:
group is the volume group this blob belongs to — the group whose rules
 admitted it. EQ-filterable because per-group quota accounting is a query
 over exactly this field plus `namespace`.

fields.name: content_hash
fields.description:
content_hash is the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the bytes, computed by this
 service AS THE UPLOAD STREAMS — native and exact. It is checked against the
 client's declared hash at end of stream and the upload fails if they
 differ (R9 step 3).

fields.name: size_bytes
fields.description: size_bytes is the byte count as counted on the wire, not as declared.

fields.name: content_type
fields.description:
content_type is what `GET /b/` serves. It survived both the group's
 allow-list and the magic-byte sniff, so it describes the stored bytes
 rather than merely what the uploader said about them.

fields.name: created_ms
fields.description:
created_ms is when the blob was promoted. RANGE-filterable: "what landed
 this week" is a question about this field, and it is what a later GC over
 consumers' pointers (R12) would scan.

fields.name: owner_principal
fields.description:
owner_principal is the OWNING SERVICE identity — docmanager, not blobstore
 — and the row's owning principal (R6). Only this identity creates or
 revokes links or deletes the blob.

 `spiffe_id` below is the record's declared owner but is the PUBLISHER,
 which is always blobstore, so it is the wrong field to filter an owner's
 reads on — the same split mailbox.MailboxEntry makes between `recipient`
 and `spiffe_id`.

fields.name: deleted
fields.description:
deleted marks the blob logically gone. The BYTES are not deleted by the
 record: the owner's Delete is what unlinks them from both pods, and this
 flag is what stops a resolve and starts the purge clock.

fields.name: spiffe_id
fields.description:
spiffe_id is the record's owner in the store's sense — the publisher, which
 is blobstore's own workload identity. See owner_principal.

fields.name: namespace
fields.description:
namespace is the OWNING TENANT (R6) and the second segment of blob_id. It
 is what makes dedup per-tenant: the same bytes under two namespaces are two
 rows and two files.
